Left out: multi-photo UI/ordering, EXIF orientation handling, and cleanup of orphaned S3 objects if a client mints a URL and never uploads.

Nothing exists yet beyond the spec, so this is pure design. The shape falls out of two things already in the doc: `govern()` is pure and every guardrail transition already flows through its return value, and quota_exceeded already shows the pattern (`if result.guardrail == "quota_exceeded": alert(...)`).

**Extend that pattern to a general alert-flags mechanism, computed inside `govern()`.** The catch is that the Observability list isn't the same taxonomy as the priority-collapsed `guardrail` field — a cycle can have `cap_clamped` win the guardrail slot while pace error is *also* over 15%, and both need to alert independently. So `govern()`'s result should carry a set of alert flags alongside the single `guardrail`, derived from counters it already threads through persisted state (the doc mentions a stale-cycle streak for `feed_stale`; add matching streak counters for cap-pinned and pace-error). The supervisor becomes a dumb loop over whichever flags came back true, calling `alert(condition, tenant)` for each — same shape as the existing line, just generalized.

Keeping detection inside `govern()` rather than in the supervisor matters because it's the only way the simulation harness (replaying recorded days at thousands of cycles/sec) can verify alerting behavior at all, not just cap values — and it keeps alert-edge cases unit-testable the same way guardrail edges already are.

One condition can't fit this: **heartbeat-missed** is the absence of a cycle running, so nothing inside the loop can detect it. That needs an external dead-man's-switch — something outside the tenant loop that expects a heartbeat every 5 minutes per tenant (or fleet-wide) and pages when one doesn't arrive.

Fork worth deciding explicitly: do the new streak counters live in the same persisted `state` blob `govern()` already owns, or does the supervisor track them separately? I'd put them in `state`, since that's where `feed_stale`'s streak already lives and it keeps all alert logic replayable through the same harness.

Every write in this service already funnels through one place: `db.write()` in db.js, which opens a single client and wraps `BEGIN`/`COMMIT`. That's the chokepoint to build on, plus Postgres triggers on the audited tables.

**Schema**: an append-only `audit_log(id, table_name, row_id, action, actor_id, account_id, occurred_at, old_row jsonb, new_row jsonb)`. Revoke `UPDATE`/`DELETE` on it from the app's DB role so a compromised app can't rewrite history. `occurred_at` defaults to `now()` at the DB, not the app clock.

**Capture point**: row-level `AFTER INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE` triggers on `accounts`, `orders`, etc., writing `OLD`/`NEW` into `audit_log` as jsonb. This is DB-enforced — it catches every write to those tables, including one run from `psql` outside the app, not just the ones you remembered to instrument in accounts.js or orders.js.

**Actor identity**: triggers can't see `req.user`. Extend `db.write()` (db.js:13) to accept the acting user and issue `SET LOCAL app.user_id = $1` as the first statement in the transaction it already opens; the trigger reads it back via `current_setting('app.user_id')`. That's a one-line change in the single write chokepoint, not one per route — accounts.js and orders.js just start passing `req.user` into `db.write(...)` alongside `text`/`params`.

**The real fork**: DB triggers vs. logging inside `db.write()` itself. App-level logging is easier to enrich with request metadata (route, IP) but only covers writes that go through this code path — anyone with direct DB access skips it silently. Triggers are DB-enforced but need the `SET LOCAL` plumbing to know who's acting. Since this is a compliance requirement ("every write"), I'd default to triggers — the guarantee needs to survive someone going around the app, not just around your route handlers.

The 900ms is explained by `db.js`: `productBySlug` (~40ms) + `relatedProducts` (~600ms, four-table join) + `stockFor` (~250ms), all in `routes/products.js:10-13`. None of it varies per user — the route comment says price, stock, and copy are identical for everyone, and catalog rows change only a few times a day.

The real problem isn't missing cache infrastructure, it's `middleware/security.js`. It sends `no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate, private` to *every* route, including `/p`, because an account-page leak (`routes/account.js`) got fixed by applying the fix app-wide. `CDN.md` confirms the CDN is already sitting in front of every request and honors whatever `Cache-Control` the origin sends — it's at 0% hit rate purely because the app tells it never to cache, and platform engineering has explicitly refused to own policy via path rules; it has to come from headers.

So: scope `security.js` so `/p` gets a cacheable, public policy and `/account` keeps the current lockdown. That alone turns the existing CDN into the cache, no new system to build. The one decision that actually forks the design is the TTL/staleness tradeoff for stock — it's the one field on the page that moves faster than "a few times a day" (it changes per order). Either accept page-level staleness up to the TTL (fine for a "few in stock" indicator, not fine if it drives an "add to cart" decision at the edge), or keep the page cached but re-fetch stock client-side/via a short-TTL fragment. Everything else on the page can safely ride a multi-minute `max-age` plus `stale-while-revalidate`, invalidated by nothing more than TTL expiry — there's no per-user variance to worry about.

Key off `req.client.client_id`, not IP — the auth middleware in `routes/api.js:7-19` already resolves it from the API key, and the file's own comment notes clients share NAT addresses, so IP-keying would throttle innocent bystanders instead of the offender.

Enforce it as a second middleware in `routes/api.js`, right after that auth block, before any request touches Postgres — Redis is already the one thing every cluster worker and every box share (`redis.js:3-4`), so it's the natural place for the shared counter; in-process counting is invisible to the other 3 workers per box (`app.js:6-7`) and would only catch 1/4 of the traffic. Use a Lua script (`EVAL`) for the increment-and-check so it's atomic under concurrent hits from the same client across workers — a bare `GET`-then-`SET` race lets the limit slip under load, which is exactly the failure mode you're trying to fix.

The real fork is fixed-window vs token-bucket. Fixed window (`INCR` + `PEXPIRE NX` on a `ratelimit:{client_id}:{windowStart}` key) is two Redis calls and easy to reason about, but lets a client burst up to 2x the limit across a window boundary. Token bucket (or sliding-log) smooths that out and is what actually stops "hammering," at the cost of a slightly meatier Lua script. Given the problem you're describing, I'd default to token bucket. Limit thresholds should come from `req.client.plan`, since that lookup is already happening. On rejection, return 429 with `Retry-After` rather than silently dropping.

Left out: what to do when Redis itself is slow or down (fail-open vs fail-closed), and whether limits apply per-route or globally across `/v1`.

WebSockets are out here — `PLATFORM.md` says connection upgrades 501 at the edge before they reach your code. SSE doesn't help either: instances freeze between invocations and functions are killed at 10s, so there's no way to hold a connection open server-side to push updates. And it wouldn't matter anyway — `rollup.md` says the data only changes once a minute, on a fixed schedule tied to the finance close window, so there's nothing to push in real time even if you could.

That leaves polling, which is really the only fit given the constraints, and `/api/metrics` is already cheap enough for it (30ms, 4KB, `no-store`). In `public/dashboard.js`, replace the click-only `load()` with a `setInterval` call to the same function, and skip the re-render when `computed_at` hasn't changed since the last poll — cheap to check, avoids flicker on the 59 out of 60 seconds nothing changed.

The one real fork: fixed-interval polling (every 15-20s) vs. schedule-aligned polling (compute the next `:00` boundary and poll a few seconds after it, so roughly once a minute). Fixed-interval is simpler and keeps working if the rollup cadence ever changes; schedule-aligned cuts request volume 3-4x but hard-codes a dependency on a schedule the doc says is fixed by finance, not by you.

Left out: pausing the interval on `visibilitychange` so backgrounded tabs stop hitting frozen serverless instances, and fetch-failure backoff — worth adding, neither changes the core design.

Grounded in what's here: `payments.js` has zero retry logic — a timeout throws straight up to `checkout.js:29`, which maps *any* error (including a bare timeout) to `payment failed`. `PROVIDER.md` says the vendor treats a timed-out charge as **unknown, never failed**, and supports an `Idempotency-Key` header we currently don't send (`payments.js` has no such header at all).

The real fork is: **retry inline in the request, or move to pending + async reconciliation.** Given the vendor's own guidance that a timeout means "unknown," I'd do the latter:

- **Idempotency key first.** Generate one key per charge *attempt* (e.g. `order.id + a stored attempt counter`), persist it on the order row before the first call to Cardstream, and reuse the same key on every retry of that attempt. This is what makes retrying safe at all — without it, a retry after a timeout risks a real double charge.
- **On timeout, don't fail — go pending.** `checkout.js` currently collapses timeout and decline into the same 502. Split them: a timeout (or 5xx/network error) sets the order to `payment_pending` and returns that to the customer, not `payment failed`. A real decline from Cardstream (4xx with a decline reason) is the only case that should say "failed."
- **Retry the pending ones out-of-band**, not in the HTTP handler — a background job re-POSTs to `/v2/charges` with the same idempotency key on a backoff schedule (a few attempts over the next minute or two covers "times out a few times a day"). Because the key is reused, Cardstream returns the original charge if it actually went through, instead of authorizing twice.
- Order status becomes a small state machine: `pending → paid | failed | payment_pending`, with `payment_pending` resolved by the retry job into `paid` or `failed`.

Left out at this depth: what the customer sees while `payment_pending` (poll vs webhook-driven UI update), and a cap/circuit-breaker so a Cardstream outage doesn't retry forever.

Direct-to-storage upload: client requests a presigned URL from your backend, uploads straight to S3/GCS from the phone, then confirms completion so the backend creates the listing-photo record (pending → active). Keeps multi-MB camera files off your app servers and works fine over flaky mobile networks since it's a single PUT with resumable/retry support.

The one decision that actually forks this: whether to resize/compress on-device before upload or accept the original and downsize server-side. Client-side (canvas or a lib like browser-image-compression) cuts upload time and mobile data usage, which matters more for camera photos than desktop ones — I'd do that plus a server-side re-encode as the source of truth, since you can't trust client output alone (orientation/EXIF, HEIC from iPhones needing conversion to JPEG/WebP).

Thumbnail/variant generation (listing card size, full-size, etc.) should run async in a worker triggered off the storage upload event, not inline in the request — depth I'm not expanding on unless you want it.

Two distinct mechanisms, because the eight conditions split into two shapes:

**Guardrail/threshold alerts** (`quota_exceeded`, `floor_at_risk`, `floor_unreachable`, `config_invalid`, `feed_stale`×3, cap-pinned×2, pace-error×2) all originate inside a single `govern()` call. I'd have `govern()` return an `alerts: []` list alongside `cap`/`state`/`guardrail`, computed from counters already living in the persisted state (feed_stale's 3-cycle counter already exists there; add matching consecutive-counters for cap-pinned and pace-error). The supervisor then just loops `for a in result.alerts: alert(a, tenant)` — no alerting logic in the supervisor itself. This keeps the alert decisions inside the pure core, so they ride the same unit-test ladder and the simulation harness replay for free, and emitting only on the threshold-crossing edge (not every cycle the condition holds) avoids repeat-alert spam without a separate dedup layer.

**Heartbeat missed** can't work this way — it's the *absence* of a `govern()` call, and code inside the loop can't detect its own non-execution. That needs an external dead-man's-switch watching the per-tenant "last cycle recorded" timestamp from step 4, firing if it hasn't advanced within ~1.5× the 5-minute cadence.

The fork worth flagging: counters for cap-pinned/pace-error could instead live as supervisor-side bookkeeping rather than core state. I lean core, since the spec's whole design already puts consecutive-cycle logic (feed_stale) there and treats supervisor purity/side-effect-freedom as the load-bearing property. Left out: the actual transport `alert()` calls into (pager vs. Slack vs. metrics-based alerting rules) and dedup/throttle policy at that layer, which is a separate decision from what triggers the call.

Two things this codebase already gives you for free: `db.write()` (db.js:13) is the single chokepoint every write passes through, and `sessionUser` (auth.js:5) resolves `req.user` on every request before any route runs. Build the audit trail off those two facts rather than instrumenting each route.

The two real forks:

**Where to capture — app-level insert vs. DB trigger.** I'd use a Postgres trigger (`AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE` per audited table, writing table, row id, operation, old/new row as jsonb, and timestamp into an append-only `audit_log`), not an extra insert inside `write()`. A trigger catches every write, including ones that bypass `db.write()` later (migrations, a future direct `psql`, an admin script), and gives you real before/after diffs via `OLD`/`NEW` without an extra `SELECT`. The tradeoff is it can't see `req.user` directly.

**Getting the actor into the trigger.** Add an actor param to `write()` and have it run `SET LOCAL app.actor_id = $1` as the first statement in the same transaction (auth.js already hands you `req.user.id`; every route already calls `db.write`, so this is a signature change at ~4 call sites, not a rewrite). The trigger reads it back with `current_setting('app.actor_id')`. Same transaction means the audit row and the write commit or roll back together — no gap.

Also revoke `UPDATE`/`DELETE` on `audit_log` from the app's DB role, so a compromised app can't rewrite its own history.

Left out, next level down: retention/export to immutable storage for compliance beyond DB-internal tamper resistance, and how the trail gets surfaced (read API vs. direct DB access for auditors).

Split `security.js`'s cache policy by route instead of applying it globally. Right now that one middleware sets `no-store` app-wide because of a 2024 finding about `/account` leaking cross-user data through an intermediary cache — but `/p` is anonymous, identical for every visitor, and comment says stock/price/copy never vary by user. The blanket rule is why the CDN sits at 0% hit rate even though it's already positioned to cache anything the app tells it to (per `CDN.md`, policy is headers-only, no edge path rules).

Recommendation: keep `/account` on the existing strict `no-store, private` policy (that finding is still valid), and give `/p/:slug` its own middleware that sets `Cache-Control: public, max-age=<N>, stale-while-revalidate=<M>`. That turns the CDN into the cache — no new infrastructure, no second place holding policy, and it kills the DB load for repeat requests to the same slug, including the 600ms join and the 250ms stock sum.

The one thing that forks this: how stale can `stockFor` be? Catalogue edits are a few times a day, so a multi-minute TTL on `productBySlug`/`relatedProducts` is clearly fine — but stock can move with every purchase, and it's baked into the same rendered response. If near-real-time stock matters (e.g., to avoid overselling display), it needs to come out of the cached page and be fetched separately (small async call or client-side fetch) rather than sharing one TTL with the rest of the page. If stale-by-a-few-minutes stock is acceptable, one TTL for the whole response is simpler and sufficient.

For the immediate problem: identify the offending client by API key (not IP — NATs and shared proxies make IP unreliable), and throttle or block just that key at whatever sits in front of `/v1` today (gateway, LB, or a quick app-level check) while you build the real thing.

For the durable system: token bucket per API key, enforced as early as possible in the request path — ideally at a gateway/proxy layer (Envoy, Kong, nginx) rather than deep in application code, so abusive traffic gets rejected before it consumes real backend resources. State needs to live somewhere shared (Redis, via an atomic `INCR`+`EXPIRE` or a Lua script) unless you're pinned to a single instance — otherwise a client bypasses the limit just by landing on a different node. On rejection, return `429` with `Retry-After` rather than silently dropping, so well-behaved clients back off instead of retrying immediately and compounding the load.

The one thing that forks this: is there already a gateway/proxy in front of `/v1`, or does every request hit the application directly? If there's a gateway, this is a config change there and you're done in an afternoon; if not, you're adding Redis-backed middleware, which is a bigger lift. What's fronting `/v1` right now?

Given the platform notes in `PLATFORM.md`, WebSockets and SSE are both off the table: connection upgrades 501 at the edge, and any long-lived response gets killed at 10s anyway since there's no sticky routing to keep reconnecting to the same warm instance. That leaves polling as the only real option, which is fine here because `/api/metrics` (`api/metrics.js:6`) is already a cheap point read (30ms, 4KB) against a table that only changes once a minute (`jobs/rollup.md:3`).

Build it as `setInterval` polling in `public/dashboard.js`, calling the same `load()` that the refresh button already calls, and skip the re-render when `computed_at` hasn't changed from the last fetch (avoids DOM churn on the ~59 minutes-worth of seconds where the rollup is stale by design). Pause the interval on `document.visibilitychange` so backgrounded tabs stop hammering the function.

The one real fork: poll interval. Tying it tightly to :00 (e.g. compute delay to next minute boundary) saves requests but couples the client to a schedule note that says it's finance-controlled and could change; a flat 15–20s interval is simpler and self-corrects if that schedule ever moves, at the cost of ~3-4x more invocations than the minimum needed. I'd pick the flat interval — the schedule coupling isn't worth the fragility for a 30ms endpoint.

The bug isn't "we need retry logic" — it's that a timeout is being treated as a decline. A timeout means the outcome is unknown; the charge may well have succeeded on the processor's side, so retrying blind risks a double charge.

Fix: send an idempotency key per checkout attempt (order/cart id), reused on every retry — the processor then dedupes and returns the original result instead of creating a second charge. On timeout, don't show "payment failed" — look up the charge by that key first; only retry (same key, short backoff) if it's genuinely absent/pending, and only surface "failed" on an actual decline response.

The fork: inline synchronous retry (hold the request, retry once or twice within the HTTP call) vs. async (return "processing", requeue a reconciliation job, resolve via webhook/poll). At "a few times a day," inline retry with the idempotency key is simplest and enough; async is the deeper answer only if timeouts are frequent or retries can run longer than your request budget. Left out: what to do if the reconciliation lookup itself times out (needs a terminal "contact support" path, not an infinite retry loop).

Depends on two forks: what you're already storing products in, and how much relevance quality you need.

**Recommendation:** if products already live in Postgres, add a `tsvector` column over name+description with a GIN index, plus `pg_trgm` for typo tolerance, and query it through a normal API endpoint — no new infrastructure. Reach for a dedicated engine (Typesense/Meilisearch, or Elasticsearch if you need heavier faceting) only past roughly 100k–1M products or once Postgres FTS can't keep latency down.

**Fork 1 — data store:** on MySQL or something without solid FTS, skip straight to Typesense/Meilisearch — self-hosting FTS workarounds there costs more than running a small search service.

**Fork 2 — relevance:** keyword/trigram matching handles "a few words" typed against name/description fine to start. Semantic queries (matching intent, not just substrings) would need embeddings + vector search layered on later — not needed for v1.

Left out: indexing/sync pipeline (how catalog updates reach the search index), ranking tie-breaks, and pagination — those are next-level-down once the store choice is settled.

**Recommendation:** client-side resize/compress each photo (canvas/`createImageBitmap`, downscale to ~2048px long edge, JPEG ~80%) before upload, then upload directly to object storage (S3/R2/GCS) via a presigned URL the API issues. Your server only creates the listing-photo DB row and signs the URL — it never touches the image bytes, so full-resolution phone camera files (often 10-50MB, HEIC) never hit your app server or its request timeout. On upload-complete, a queued job strips EXIF (GPS especially) and generates thumbnail/display variants.

Two decisions actually fork this:
- **Resumability** — sellers uploading over spotty mobile data means a plain presigned PUT just fails on drop. tus or S3 multipart adds resume-on-reconnect at the cost of more client complexity; worth it if this is mobile-web/PWA rather than a native app with better upload primitives.
- **Where variants get generated** — a storage-triggered function (Lambda/Cloud Function on object-create) stays fully decoupled from your app; a job on a queue you already run is less new infrastructure.

Bucket/key layout, serving via CDN vs signed GET URLs, and per-listing photo limits are the next level down.

Don't build this as 8 scattered `alert()` call sites (the pseudocode's inline `alert("quota exceeded", ...)` doesn't scale, and it can't express the "N consecutive cycles" conditions on its own). Instead:

- Have the supervisor emit one structured event per cycle — tenant, cap, guardrail fired, pace error, and the consecutive-cycle counters that `govern()`'s persisted state already has to track anyway (stale-cycle count, pin count, pace-error count) since the guardrail logic depends on them. Route that event stream to your metrics/alerting system and define the 6 single- and multi-cycle conditions (`quota_exceeded`, `floor_at_risk`, `floor_unreachable`, `config_invalid`, `feed_stale`×3, cap-pinned×2, pace-error×2) as threshold rules there, not as code paths in the loop.
- Heartbeat-missed is a different shape of problem: it's the *absence* of a cycle, which nothing inside a loop that didn't run can detect. That needs a dead-man's-switch outside the per-tenant loop — the supervisor pings a liveness check each cycle, and a separate monitor alerts when a tenant's expected 5-minute ping doesn't show up.

The fork that actually matters: whether alert-worthy state (the consecutive-cycle counters) lives only in `govern()`'s persisted state or gets duplicated in the alerting system. Keep it in one place — persisted controller state — and have the emitted event just carry it through, so the two "sources of truth" stay in sync automatically.

Grounding this in what's here: every write already funnels through `db.write()` in db.js:13-26 (comment says as much — "exactly one place a transaction begins"), and `req.user` is set once by `sessionUser` in auth.js. Routes (accounts.js, orders.js) call `db.write(text, params)` with no actor or table metadata attached.

**Recommendation: enforce the audit trail at the database with a generic trigger, not in application code.** `db.write()` only covers writes made through this app — migrations, a `psql` console, or a future service hitting the same DB would silently bypass an app-level logger. Compliance wants "every write," so the guarantee has to live where writes can't avoid it: a `BEFORE`/`AFTER` trigger on each audited table, calling one shared trigger function that serializes `OLD`/`NEW` as jsonb into an append-only `audit_log` table (`table_name, row_id, action, old_row, new_row, actor_id, changed_at`). One line (`CREATE TRIGGER ... EXECUTE FUNCTION audit_row()`) per table to opt it in.

**The one thing that genuinely forks the design: how the trigger learns "who."** Postgres triggers only see the row change, not the HTTP session. Fix it in `db.write()`, since that's already the single chokepoint that opens the transaction: before running the caller's query, do `SET LOCAL app.user_id = $1` using `req.user.id` (passed in as a new `db.write(text, params, actor)` argument from each route). The trigger reads it back with `current_setting('app.user_id', true)`. This keeps route code almost unchanged (accounts.js:7, orders.js:7/15 just add `req.user.id`) while making the actor available to any write regardless of which SQL runs — updates, deletes, raw migrations run through the same pool.

Left out at this depth, worth deciding next: locking `audit_log` down to `INSERT`-only (`REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE` from the app's DB role) so the trail can't be edited after the fact, and retention/export policy for compliance pulls.

Cache the product data layer, not the rendered page: on read, check Redis for the assembled product record by ID (`product:{id}`); on miss, hit the DB and populate it with a TTL of a few minutes as a safety net. On write, invalidate the specific key directly in the update path rather than relying on TTL expiry alone, so price/stock changes show up immediately.

This resolves the main fork — cache the DB result vs. cache the whole rendered page. Since the DB accounts for nearly all 900ms, caching just the data already removes most of the latency, and rendering stays per-request so personalization (pricing tiers, A/B tests, session-specific content) still works normally. Caching full HTML would shave a bit more but forces you to solve invalidation and personalization at the page level, which is a much bigger lift for little extra gain here.

Left out: key design for locale/currency variants, and how invalidation should propagate if inventory updates come from a different service than the write path.

Recommendation: a Redis-backed counter keyed by `client_id`, enforced as middleware in `routes/api.js` right after the existing auth block resolves `req.client`, returning `429` with `Retry-After` when exceeded.

Two decisions actually fork this, given what's in the repo:

1. **Key on `client_id`, not IP.** The auth middleware comment says one client calls from many addresses and several clients share an address behind NAT — IP-based limiting would both miss the noisy client and collaterally throttle innocent ones sharing its IP. `req.client.client_id` is already resolved before the route handlers run, so the limiter slots in right after that DB lookup.

2. **State has to live in Redis, not process memory.** `app.js` runs 4 cluster workers per box with nothing shared in module scope — an in-memory counter would let each worker (times however many boxes) grant the limit separately, so the client could hammer `/v1` at N× the intended rate. `redis.js` already says Redis is "the only piece of state the workers have in common," so it's the natural place: `INCR` a `ratelimit:{client_id}:{window}` key with `PEXPIRE` on first increment (or a small Lua script if you want the increment+expire atomic under race).

Left out at this depth: bucket shape (fixed window vs. sliding window vs. token bucket — fixed window via INCR/EXPIRE is simplest and usually enough), the actual limit numbers per plan (the `plan` column from `api_keys` is already fetched, so tiering is free), and whether to rate-limit `/v1` globally per client or per-route.

Polling, not push — `PLATFORM.md` rules out WebSockets (connection upgrades 501 at the edge) and SSE (instances are frozen between invocations, and a 10s function timeout would kill the stream anyway). Client-side `setInterval` calling the existing `/api/metrics` endpoint is the only option this platform allows.

The one real design choice is interval and redraw logic: `rollup` only changes once a minute (`jobs/rollup.md`), so polling faster just adds load without new data. Poll every 15–20s, but compare the returned `computed_at` to the last one rendered and skip the redraw if it hasn't changed — `dashboard.js`'s `load()` already returns `computed_at`, so this is a small change to that function, not a new endpoint. `api/metrics.js` stays as-is; it's already cheap (4KB/30ms) and already sends `no-store`.

Left out: pausing the interval on `visibilitychange` for backgrounded tabs — worth adding but a separate, smaller decision.

The core fix isn't "retry the charge" — it's stop treating a timeout as a failure. Two things fork the design:

**1. Idempotency key on every attempt.** Generate one key per checkout attempt and send it with the original charge and every retry. The processor then guarantees "same key = same charge processed once," so a retry after a timeout can never double-charge, even if the original request actually succeeded on their end and only the response was lost.

**2. Retryable vs. not.** A timeout or 5xx/network error means *unknown outcome* — retry it. A decline (insufficient funds, fraud block) is a *known* outcome — never retry that, show it as a real failure. Right now you're likely collapsing both into "payment failed," which is the actual customer-facing bug.

Given it's "a few times a day," the cheap fix is: on timeout, retry inline 1-2 times with the same idempotency key and short backoff before ever telling the customer anything; only show "payment failed" if a retry comes back with an actual decline, or all retries still time out. That's a synchronous retry, invisible to the customer.

The one thing that forks it further: if a timeout can take longer than the customer will wait on the checkout page, inline retry isn't enough — you need to return "processing" immediately, do the retry in a background job, and push the final result via webhook/poll. Do you know whether your timeouts resolve in seconds or can hang longer than that?

For a catalog in the thousands-to-low-hundred-thousands range, skip new infra: use Postgres full-text search (`tsvector`/`tsquery` over name+description, GIN index) plus `pg_trgm` for typo tolerance and prefix matching. That's the whole system — no separate index to keep in sync.

The fork is catalog size and stack. If it's millions of products, needs faceting/filters, or you want relevance tuning beyond what Postgres offers, move to a dedicated engine — Meilisearch or Typesense for low ops overhead, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch if you need more power and already run that kind of infra. If "matching" should mean semantic similarity rather than keyword overlap, that's a different fork entirely (embeddings + vector search), and requires knowing whether shoppers search by attribute words or descriptive phrases.

I left out ranking/boosting rules and indexing pipeline (batch vs on-write) — that's the next layer once the scale/semantic decision is made. What's the expected catalog size, and is Postgres already in the stack?

Direct-to-storage is the right shape here: client asks the backend for a presigned upload URL (S3/GCS/R2), uploads straight to object storage, then confirms completion back to the backend — the app server never touches the multipart body, which matters once sellers are pushing multiple 3-12MB phone photos per listing. On the backend, create a pending photo record before the upload (owner, listing, status) so orphaned uploads can be swept, and flip it to attached on the completion callback.

Two decisions actually fork this:
- **Where resizing happens.** Client-side downscale before upload (faster perceived UX, less bandwidth, but inconsistent across phone browsers/HEIC support) vs. server-side only (reliable, but needs an async job — queue triggered on upload-complete that transcodes HEIC→JPEG, strips EXIF/GPS, generates thumbnail + display sizes). Most listing apps do both: a quick client-side downscale for upload speed, then authoritative server-side processing for the variants actually served.
- **Validation point.** Whether you trust the presigned URL alone (rely on storage bucket policy for size/type limits) or add a lightweight server-side check on the completion callback before marking the photo attached (reject if not an image, wrong dimensions, malware scan). Worth doing if listings are public-facing.

Left out: ordering/reordering photos within a listing, and moderation (auto or manual) before a photo goes live — both are next-level-down concerns once the upload path itself is settled.

Two different alert shapes are hiding in that Observability list, and they don't fit through the same pipe.

Five of the eight conditions are just `result.guardrail` values from a single cycle (`quota_exceeded`, `floor_at_risk`, `floor_unreachable`, `config_invalid`, and `feed_stale` past its fallback) — the supervisor loop already has `result` in hand, so these extend the existing `if result.guardrail == "quota_exceeded": alert(...)` line into a small dispatch table, same pattern SPEC.md already shows.

The other three need memory across cycles that a single `govern()` call doesn't have on its own: cap pinned for two cycles, pace error >15% for two cycles, and missed heartbeat. Since `govern()` is deliberately pure (SPEC.md:37-42, and the simulation harness depends on that staying true), the fork is where that memory lives:
- Cheapest option: fold pin-count and pace-error-count into the same persisted controller `state` govern() already returns (it's already doing this for `feed_stale`'s three-cycle counter), and have the supervisor just compare the returned counters to thresholds. Alert decisions stay reproducible by the simulation harness for free, no second store to keep in sync.
- Alternative: keep a separate supervisor-side alert-state (per tenant, per condition) outside `govern()`. Needed for anything that isn't visible inside a normal cycle — heartbeat-missed is the one case that genuinely requires this, since if the loop never runs, nothing inside the loop can raise it. That has to be an external watchdog (cron-expectation check or dead-man's-switch on last-run timestamp), independent of the control loop.

Recommendation: extend `govern()`'s state for the two consecutive-cycle counters (keeps them replayable and testable the same way guardrails already are), and add a standalone heartbeat watchdog outside the loop for the missed-heartbeat case. `alert()` itself is a thin side-effecting adapter in the supervisor, unchanged in spirit from the pseudocode.

Left out: alert delivery mechanics (pager vs Slack vs webhook) and de-dup/resolution semantics (don't re-page every 5 minutes for a still-ongoing condition) — worth designing but not fork points.

Both writes in this service already funnel through one place — `db.write()` in `db.js:13` — so that's the chokepoint to instrument rather than touching every route handler.

**Core approach:** extend `write()` to take a table/id and record an audit row in the same transaction as the write itself (right between `BEGIN` and `COMMIT` in `db.js:16-18`), so an audit entry can never be committed without its write, or vice versa. Capture: actor, table, row id, action (insert/update/delete), old value, new value, and timestamp, as one JSONB-friendly row in an append-only `audit_log` table.

Two decisions actually fork this:

1. **How "who" reaches `write()`.** Route handlers never pass `req` into `db.js`, and `req.user` is already resolved once in `auth.js:11` for every request. Rather than adding a `user` argument to every one of the ~4 call sites (and every future one), set the actor in `AsyncLocalStorage` inside `sessionUser`, and have `write()` read it from there. This also protects you against someone adding a new route that forgets to pass an actor.
2. **Where "before" comes from.** `UPDATE ... RETURNING *` only gives the *new* row. For a real diff you need the old row too — either a `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` immediately before the mutation inside the same transaction, or push the whole thing to Postgres triggers that snapshot `OLD`/`NEW` on every table. Triggers are the safer bet for compliance since they also catch any write that bypasses `db.write()` (a raw `pool.query`, a migration, a psql session) — application-level capture only sees what goes through your code.

Given this is a small service with a single write chokepoint already, I'd do capture at the application layer for simplicity and rich context (you get the authenticated user, not just a DB role), but add triggers as a backstop only for tables where "was this ever changed outside the app" itself matters for compliance.

Rounding it out: make `audit_log` genuinely append-only (`REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE` for the app's DB role, maybe a separate write-only role), and decide retention up front since compliance audits usually specify a minimum (e.g., 7 years) that outlives normal data-retention policy on the tables themselves.

Reading the code: the 900ms is `relatedProducts` (~600ms) + `stockFor` (~250ms) + `productBySlug` (~40ms), all per-request DB hits with no caching layer (db.js:4-20). The CDN in front of everything is sitting at 0% hit rate not because it's absent but because `security.js` sets `no-store` on every response app-wide (app.js:9, middleware/security.js:8) — a blanket fix for a 2024 finding where an *account* page (per-user, session-bound) leaked into a shared cache. Product pages are the opposite case: anonymous, identical for every visitor, changing only a few times a day per the comment in routes/products.js:6-8.

The fix is to stop applying one Cache-Control policy globally and instead make it per-route: keep `no-store` on `/account` (that's the actual audit constraint, don't touch it), and set something like `Cache-Control: public, max-age=300` on `/p` responses. The CDN already respects whatever the origin sends, so this alone lets it start serving repeat product-page requests without hitting the DB at all — no new infrastructure, just fixing the header that's currently suppressing the cache that's already there.

One real tradeoff: `stockFor` is inventory, which likely moves faster than "a few times a day." Caching the whole page publicly means stock can read stale for up to the TTL. If that's not acceptable, the next-level-down design is splitting the cached page shell from a live/short-TTL stock fetch — worth deciding once you know how stale stock is allowed to get.

Two moves here: stop the bleeding now, then build the general mechanism.

**Now**: identify the offending client (API key, token, or IP if unauthenticated) from your access logs, and throttle or block just that key at the edge — a quick nginx/gateway rule or WAF rule buys time without touching app code.

**The general system**: rate limit per client identity (API key/account, not raw IP — IPs get shared behind NATs and proxies) using a **token bucket**, since it allows reasonable bursts while capping sustained rate — a fixed-window counter is simpler but lets clients double their rate by hammering the window boundary. Store the bucket state in Redis with an atomic Lua script (INCR+EXPIRE or GCRA) so it's correct across multiple app instances, not just in-process memory. On exceeding the limit, return `429` with a `Retry-After` header rather than silently dropping requests. Track per-client usage as a metric so you can see clients approaching their limit before they blow through it.

The fork I can't resolve without knowing your infra: if you already run a gateway/reverse proxy (nginx, Envoy, Kong) in front of `/v1`, the limiter belongs there as a policy, not in app code; if it's a bare app fleet with no gateway, it becomes middleware backed by Redis. Which is it?

Given the platform constraints in `PLATFORM.md`, this rules out the usual push options: WebSocket upgrades return 501 at the edge, and functions are frozen/killed at 10s, so nothing can hold a connection open for SSE or long-polling either. Since `rollup` only changes once a minute (`jobs/rollup.md`) and `/api/metrics` is already cheap (4KB, ~30ms), plain client-side polling on an interval is the right fit here, not a real fork.

In `public/dashboard.js`, replace the click-only wiring with a `setInterval(load, …)` alongside the existing `load()` call, keeping the same `/api/metrics` fetch.

Two decisions actually worth making:
- **Interval**: poll every 15–20s rather than trying to sync to the top of the minute — simpler, and `Cache-Control: no-store` means every poll hits the DB anyway, so there's no caching upside to precise timing.
- **Skip no-op re-renders**: compare the fetched `computed_at` to the last one before calling `render(rows)`, so the UI doesn't repaint 3-4x for every actual data change.

Optional but cheap: pause the interval on `visibilitychange` when the tab is hidden, since there's no reason to keep polling a backgrounded tab.

The real bug isn't "no retry" — it's that a timeout is being treated as a failure when it's actually unknown (the charge may have gone through on the processor's side and the response just didn't come back). Retrying blind risks double-charging.

Fix: give every charge attempt an idempotency key tied to the order (order_id + attempt), and pass it to the gateway on every call, retry included. The gateway then returns the original result instead of creating a second charge, so retrying becomes safe.

The one real fork is where the retry happens:
- **Synchronous** — catch the timeout, retry the same idempotent request 2-3x with backoff, then respond to the customer. Simple, fine if the gateway usually recovers in seconds.
- **Async** — show the customer "processing," retry/reconcile in the background via webhook or a status-poll job, and update the order when it resolves. Needed if timeouts can run longer, or you don't want the checkout request hanging open.

Given "a few times a day," start synchronous with a bounded retry (2-3 attempts, short backoff), and only fall back to the async/pending path if it's still unresolved after that — covers the quick blips without leaving the customer stuck waiting on a slow one.

Left out: exact backoff/attempt tuning, the webhook/reconciliation job for the async fallback, and logging the retry outcomes so the timeouts themselves are visible instead of silently absorbed.

Depends on what you're running product data on today, which is the one fork I can't resolve without knowing your stack — what's the current database (Postgres, MySQL, something else) and roughly how many products?

Assuming Postgres and a catalog under ~1M rows: add a `tsvector` column combining name (weighted higher) and description, index it with GIN, and query with `plainto_tsquery`/`websearch_to_tsquery`. Pair it with `pg_trgm` if you want typo tolerance on partial words. No new infrastructure, keeps search transactionally consistent with writes via a trigger or generated column.

If the catalog is much larger, you need fuzzy/typo tolerance beyond trigram, or you'll want faceted filters and sub-50ms latency, that points to a dedicated search service (Typesense or Meilisearch for low ops overhead, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch if you need more power) with the product index kept in sync via an async job on writes.

Left out at this depth: ranking tuning (recency, popularity boosts), synonym handling, and autocomplete — worth scoping once the storage decision is made.

Recommended architecture:

- Client picks/takes photos via `<input type="file" accept="image/*" multiple>` (add `capture="environment"` to bias toward the camera on mobile).
- Before upload, resize/compress in the browser (canvas or a lib like `browser-image-compression`) down to something like a 2048px long edge, and convert HEIC to JPEG — iPhone photos default to HEIC and to 12+MP files, neither of which you want going over cellular data or sitting unconverted in storage.
- Upload each file directly to object storage (S3/GCS/R2) via a presigned URL your API issues, rather than proxying the bytes through your app server. Have the client mark the listing's photo record "uploaded" once the PUT succeeds.
- On the backend, react to the upload (S3 event or a confirm call) to strip EXIF (phone photos carry GPS coordinates — you don't want a seller's home location leaking), validate it's really an image, and generate the thumbnail/display variants you'll actually serve, fronted by a CDN.

Two decisions that actually fork this:

- **Direct-to-storage vs. through your server**: direct upload with presigned URLs, because phone camera files are tens of MB and routing that through your API server just to relay it to storage burns memory/bandwidth for no benefit.
- **Where resizing happens**: do it in both places — client-side compression before upload for a faster mobile-data experience, and server-side variant generation as the source of truth, since you can't trust every client (a plain API call, a future mobile app) to have done it.

Left out: resumable/chunked upload for flaky mobile networks (tus protocol is the standard answer), content moderation, and reorder/primary-photo UI — happy to go deeper on any of those.

Building on the existing `govern()`/supervisor split (SPEC.md:10-42):

**Extend `govern()`'s return value, don't reuse `guardrail`.** The guardrail field is single-valued and priority-ordered because it drives one decision (the cap). But six of the eight alert conditions (SPEC.md:64-73) aren't the winning guardrail — `cap_clamped` isn't even in the alert list, while `feed_stale>3 cycles`, `cap pinned 2 cycles`, and `pace error >15% for 2 cycles` aren't guardrails at all, they're persistence conditions over guardrail/metric history. Multiple can be true in the same cycle (e.g. `floor_at_risk` and pace error), so alerting needs its own independent, non-priority-ordered field — e.g. `result.conditions: Set<Condition>` — computed alongside the cap inside `govern()`, keeping it pure and unit-testable the same way the guardrails are. The supervisor then just loops `for c in result.conditions: alert(c, tenant)`.

**Heartbeat-missed can't come from `govern()`.** If the loop didn't run, `govern()` never executed, so this has to be an external dead-man's-switch — something watching the persisted per-tenant cycle timestamp and firing if it's stale beyond the 5-minute period (regardless of quota/cap state).

Left out: alert dedup/paging policy (edge-triggered vs. repeat-until-clear), and which sink `alert()` writes to.

Both writes in this service funnel through one place — `db.write()` in db.js:13-26 — and every request already gets `req.user` set in auth.js before reaching a route. That combination is what makes this tractable without touching every route file.

**Recommended shape:**

1. A generic Postgres trigger, not app-level INSERTs, captures the audit rows. One trigger function attached to each table that needs coverage:

```sql
create table audit_log (
  id bigserial primary key,
  table_name text not null,
  row_id text not null,
  action text not null,           -- INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE
  actor_id text,
  old_row jsonb,
  new_row jsonb,
  changed_at timestamptz not null default now()
);

create function audit_row() returns trigger as $$
begin
  insert into audit_log(table_name, row_id, action, actor_id, old_row, new_row)
  values (TG_TABLE_NAME, coalesce(NEW.id, OLD.id)::text, TG_OP,
          current_setting('app.user_id', true),
          case when TG_OP <> 'INSERT' then row_to_json(OLD) end,
          case when TG_OP <> 'DELETE' then row_to_json(NEW) end);
  return NEW;
end;
$$ language plpgsql;

create trigger accounts_audit after insert or update or delete on accounts
  for each row execute function audit_row();
```

2. `db.write()` sets who's acting, once, right after `BEGIN`: `client.query("SET LOCAL app.user_id = $1", [actorId])`. `SET LOCAL` is transaction-scoped, so it's safe to reuse pooled connections and rolls back with everything else on failure.

**Two decisions that actually fork this:**

- **Trigger vs. app-level logging.** A trigger fires on every write to the table regardless of code path (future routes, migrations, a psql session), and gets both old and new row state for free via `OLD`/`NEW`. App-level logging inside `write()` only has the `RETURNING` row (the "new" state) — capturing "old" would mean an extra `SELECT` before every write, and every new table added later needs someone to remember to log it. Trigger wins for a compliance guarantee.
- **How "who" reaches `write()`.** `write()` only takes `(text, params)` today; it doesn't see `req`. Threading `req.user.id` as an explicit third argument means updating both route files now and every route after — visible, but one missed call site silently logs `actor_id = null`. The alternative is `AsyncLocalStorage`, set once in `sessionUser` (auth.js:5), read inside `write()` with zero call-site changes anywhere — no route can forget it. For an audit trail specifically, "can't be silently skipped" outweighs "explicit," so I'd use ALS and give it a `'system'` fallback for non-request contexts (migrations, cron jobs) rather than a null.

Left out at this depth: the migration that adds `audit_log` and the per-table triggers, retention/partitioning as the table grows, and whether `audit_log` itself needs redaction rules before compliance can query it.

Both bottlenecks are self-inflicted, not architectural gaps:

**The CDN is already positioned to do most of the work but is disabled.** `security.js` slaps `no-store` on every route, including `/p`, because of an account-page audit finding that only applies to `/account`. Nothing on the product page varies by user (comment in `products.js` confirms this), so the real fix is splitting that middleware: `/account` keeps `no-store`, `/p` gets a real `Cache-Control: public, max-age=...`. The CDN already obeys origin headers and sits in front of every request, so this alone turns repeat hits into edge hits with zero DB time, no new infrastructure.

**For the remaining misses**, add an app-level cache (Redis, or in-process if a single instance) in front of `relatedProducts` (the 600ms four-table join) and `stockFor`, keyed by product id. TTL rather than event-driven invalidation is enough — catalogue edits are a few times a day and stock is an aggregate sum, not per-user, so a few minutes of staleness is cheap and matches how infrequently the underlying data actually moves.

The fork you'll need to resolve: how stale stock is allowed to look on the product page (display only, not checkout) — that number picks the TTL for both the CDN header and the backend cache entry.

Given the setup here (`app.js` clusters 4 worker processes per box with no shared memory, `redis.js` already provides one Redis shared across every worker, and `routes/api.js` resolves each request's API key to a `client_id`/`plan` via Postgres) the shape is pretty determined:

**Key it on `client_id`, not IP.** The comment in `api.js` says one client can call from many addresses and several clients can share an address behind a NAT — IP-keyed limiting would either miss the abusive client or punish innocent ones sharing its IP. `client_id` is already resolved in the auth middleware, so it's free to key on.

**Store counters in Redis, not in-process.** `express-rate-limit`'s default memory store (or any per-process counter) won't work — the 4 cluster workers are separate processes with separate heaps, and there's likely more than one box behind the load balancer. Redis is already the one thing every worker shares, so a Lua script (`INCR` + `PEXPIRE`, or a token bucket if you want smoother burst handling) keyed on `client_id`, with limits scaled by `plan`, is the natural fit. Return `429` + `Retry-After` on trip, and fail open (let requests through) if Redis errors, so the limiter can't itself become an outage.

One thing worth flagging: the auth middleware does a Postgres query on *every* request with no caching, so a client hammering `/v1` is also hammering the `pg` pool that every other client's requests wait on — that's a big part of "degrading it for everybody else." Put the rate-limit check in that same middleware, right after `req.client` is resolved (or ahead of it, if you cache `api_keys` lookups in Redis by key), so an over-limit client gets turned away before costing another DB round trip.

Left out: the exact algorithm (fixed-window vs token bucket) and per-plan limit numbers, and whether the limit applies to all of `/v1` or per-route.

Two viable approaches, forking on how fresh the data needs to be and how much backend change you can tolerate:

- **Polling**: client re-fetches on an interval (e.g. every 10-30s) with conditional requests (ETag / `If-Modified-Since`) so unchanged data doesn't re-render. Minimal backend change, works with any REST API, slight staleness window.
- **Push (SSE or WebSocket)**: server holds the connection open and sends updates as they happen. Near-instant, but requires the backend to support long-lived connections and emit events on state change (e.g. from a message queue or DB trigger), which is more infrastructure.

For most ops dashboards, SSE is the sweet spot — one-directional (server to client, which is all a dashboard needs), simpler than WebSockets, and works over plain HTTP. Reach for full WebSockets only if the dashboard also needs to send data back (e.g. acking an alert) or if you need sub-second latency at high message rates.

The fork you'd need to resolve: does the underlying data change get produced as a discrete event somewhere (a job finishing, a metric crossing a threshold), or is it just a value that drifts continuously (e.g. a gauge)? Event-driven data pushes cleanly over SSE; continuously-drifting data is often simplest left on a short poll.

No codebase here to derive this from, so this is generic architecture, not tailored to your stack.

**Core fix:** stop treating "timeout" as "failed." A timeout means unknown state — the charge may have gone through on the processor's side even though your request didn't get a response. The retry design has to handle that first, or you risk double-charging.

- Before calling the processor, write a `payment_attempts` row (idempotency key, order/customer id, status=`pending`) so the attempt is durable before the network call happens — a crash mid-call is then recoverable instead of orphaned.
- Use the processor's idempotency-key support (Stripe, etc. have this natively) so a retry with the same key either returns the original result or safely creates one charge, never two.
- On timeout, retry with that same key — the processor will tell you if it already has a matching charge, resolving the "did it actually succeed" question instead of guessing.
- Only retry retryable failures (timeout, network error, 5xx). Declines, insufficient funds, and other terminal errors should not retry — surface those immediately as real failures.
- Bounded exponential backoff with jitter, capped attempts.

**The fork that matters:** synchronous bounded retry inside the request vs. async queue-and-notify. At "a few times a day" volume, doing one fast synchronous retry (same idempotency key) and falling back to an async job for anything still unresolved is simplest to build and enough — you don't need a full queue-based system for this volume. If volume were higher or the processor were slower, async-only (return "processing" immediately, notify via webhook/email on outcome) would be the better fit.

Left out: exact backoff timing, webhook signature verification, and how you reconcile attempts that time out on the *reconciliation* check too — worth a follow-up once you pick the sync/async fork.

At 38k rows on Postgres 16, this doesn't need a separate search engine — Postgres full-text search on the existing table is the right scale.

**Approach**: add a generated `tsvector` column combining `name` (weighted 'A') and `description` (weighted 'B'), with a GIN index:

```sql
ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN search_vector tsvector
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
    setweight(to_tsvector('english', name), 'A') ||
    setweight(to_tsvector('english', coalesce(description, '')), 'B')
  ) STORED;
CREATE INDEX products_search_idx ON products USING GIN (search_vector);
```

New route, `GET /products/search?q=...`, using `websearch_to_tsquery` (handles multi-word input the way users actually type it) and `ts_rank` to order by relevance, still filtered on `active`:

```sql
SELECT id, sku, name, price_cents,
       ts_rank(search_vector, websearch_to_tsquery('english', $1)) AS rank
FROM products
WHERE active AND search_vector @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english', $1)
ORDER BY rank DESC
LIMIT 50;
```

The one real fork: full-text (`tsvector`) matches whole words and ranks by relevance, but won't match typos or partial substrings ("lampp" or "lam" won't hit "lamp"). If typo-tolerance matters for this product, `pg_trgm` trigram indexes are the alternative — better for fuzzy/partial matching, weaker at multi-word relevance ranking. Given this is word-based name/description search, start with full-text; add trigram later only if users report misses from typos.

The nginx config is the constraint that shapes this: `client_max_body_size 1m` is global and deliberately not overridable per-location, set that way to keep the PCI surface on `/pay/` small. A phone photo is routinely 3-8MB, so routing upload bytes through the storefront listener at all is a non-starter — not something to fix by asking for a bump.

`storage.js` already points at the answer: it supports signed PUT (same client, same helper, just `method: 'PUT'`), and the bucket's CORS already allows PUT from `market.example.com`. So the upload goes direct-to-S3, bypassing nginx's body cap entirely:

1. Client asks the storefront for a signed PUT URL for a new key (tiny JSON request, well under 1m).
2. Client PUTs the photo bytes straight to S3, not through the proxy.
3. Client tells the storefront the upload finished; storefront calls the existing `db.addPhotoKey(id, key)` to append it to `listings.photo_keys`.

The one real fork: whether step 3 trusts the client's "done" signal or the storefront verifies the object exists (HEAD request) before writing the key — trusting the client is simpler but lets a listing claim a photo key that was never actually uploaded.

Left out at this level: per-listing multi-photo handling (repeat the flow per file), EXIF-orientation/HEIC handling on upload, and constraining the presigned PUT to content-type/size via S3 policy conditions.

Alerting has two different shapes here, and the spec's own design gives you the pattern for both:

**Threshold-crossing conditions** (`feed_stale` past 3 cycles, cap pinned 2 cycles, pace error >15% for 2 cycles, plus the direct ones — `quota_exceeded`, `floor_at_risk`, `floor_unreachable`, `config_invalid`) all derive from consecutive-cycle state. `govern()` already tracks a consecutive-count for `feed_stale` (that's how it knows to fall back after three cycles), so the natural move is to extend that same persisted state to count the other conditions too, and have `govern()`'s return value include which alert-worthy flags newly crossed their threshold this cycle. The supervisor stays exactly as pseudocoded — `if result.<flag>: alert(...)` — so `govern()` stays pure and testable, and the supervisor remains the only thing that does I/O.

**Heartbeat missed** doesn't fit that loop at all — it's the absence of a cycle, so nothing inside the cycle can detect it. That needs an external watchdog (dead-man's-switch style) checking per-tenant "did a cycle get recorded in the last 5 minutes," independent of `govern()`.

The one real fork to decide: alert dedup. Firing `alert()` every single cycle a condition persists (e.g., `quota_exceeded` held at zero for hours) will spam. Either the supervisor suppresses repeat alerts for an already-firing condition (edge-triggered, alert only when the flag turns true), or the alerting backend handles dedup/grouping. Given `govern()` is already the source of truth for state transitions, edge-triggering in the supervisor off `govern()`'s output is the cleaner fit.

Every write in this service already funnels through one place: `db.write()` in `db.js:13-26`, which opens `BEGIN`/`COMMIT` around a single query. That's the chokepoint to hook, rather than instrumenting each route (`routes/accounts.js`, `routes/orders.js`) individually.

**Recommendation:** capture the audit trail in two layers, not one — the transaction boundary for *who*, Postgres triggers for *what changed*.

- **Who:** `sessionUser` in `auth.js:5-13` already resolves `req.user` on every request. Thread `req.user.id` into `db.write()` via `AsyncLocalStorage` (set once in the middleware, read inside `write()`) so route handlers don't need to pass it explicitly. Inside the existing `BEGIN` block, run `SET LOCAL app.actor_id = $1` before the real query — this ties the actor to the transaction itself, not to the call site.
- **What/when:** add an `AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE` trigger on each table that matters (`accounts`, `orders`, ...), writing `to_jsonb(OLD)`, `to_jsonb(NEW)`, `TG_OP`, `current_setting('app.actor_id')`, and `now()` into an append-only `audit_log` table. Revoke `UPDATE`/`DELETE` on `audit_log` from the app's DB role so the trail can't be edited even by a compromised app.

The two decisions that actually fork this design:

1. **Where the diff is captured** — app-level wrapper around `write()` vs. DB triggers. A wrapper is simpler but `write(text, params)` takes raw SQL with no notion of table/row, so every call site would need to pass metadata anyway. Triggers get old/new values for free and also catch writes that bypass the app entirely (migrations, psql, another service) — the compliance ask ("every write") makes that coverage worth the extra migration work.

For the counter itself: a fixed window (`INCR` + `EXPIRE` on a `ratelimit:<client_id>:<window>` key) is one Lua-free round trip and is fine if occasional boundary bursts are tolerable; a token bucket is smoother but needs a small Lua script for atomicity. Left out: the actual limit numbers per plan, and whether `/v1/reports` GET and POST should share one budget or be limited separately.

The fork that decides this: push-based (WebSocket/SSE) vs. polling. Polling is simpler and fine if a few seconds of staleness is acceptable — the frontend just re-fetches on an interval and diffs the result. Push is better if the dashboard needs near-real-time updates or the refresh volume would hammer the backend, but it needs a transport (SSE for one-way server-to-client, WebSocket if the dashboard also sends things back) and a way to fan out change events from wherever the underlying data changes (DB triggers, a message queue, or the write path itself publishing an event).

Given you're often near real-time-ish ops data, I'd lean SSE unless you already have WebSocket infra — it's simpler to run behind normal HTTP/load balancers and you don't need bidirectional messaging for a dashboard.

What's the dashboard's current stack (frontend framework, backend, and where the underlying metrics/data live)? That determines whether push is cheap to add or whether polling is the pragmatic choice.

The fix here is idempotency + reconciliation, not just "add a retry loop" — a timeout means the charge outcome is *unknown*, not failed, and blindly retrying without protection risks double-charging the card.

Core pieces:
- **Idempotency key per charge attempt**, generated once client-side and reused across retries (Stripe, Braintree, Adyen all support this natively). This is what makes retrying safe.
- **On timeout, reconcile before retrying** — query the provider for the status of that idempotency key rather than assuming failure. Half the "few times a day" timeouts are probably charges that actually succeeded but the response never made it back.
- **Retry policy lives server-side**, exponential backoff, capped attempts (e.g. 3 tries over ~30s), not left to the client — a flaky client connection shouldn't be what triggers duplicate submissions.

The one real fork: is the customer waiting synchronously on this request? If timeouts resolve in a few seconds, you can hold the connection through a bounded retry/reconcile loop and return the real result. If not, return "processing" immediately and confirm success/failure asynchronously via webhook or a status poll — better UX than either a long hang or a false "payment failed."

Separately, the current bug is that timeout is being mapped straight to the generic failure message — that's worth fixing regardless of the retry design, since it's actively lying to customers about charges that may have gone through.

The core fork: Postgres full-text search versus a dedicated search engine (Typesense, Meilisearch, OpenSearch/Elasticsearch).

If the catalog already lives in Postgres, add a generated `tsvector` column over name + description, index it with GIN, and rank results with `ts_rank`. No new infrastructure, handles catalogs into the hundreds of thousands of rows with sub-50ms queries, and updates automatically on write.

Reach for a dedicated engine only if you need typo tolerance, faceted filters, or the catalog/query volume is large enough that Postgres FTS starts showing up in slow-query logs — that adds an indexing pipeline to keep it in sync with the source of truth, which is real ongoing cost.

What's the product catalog's datastore today? That's the fork that decides between "add a column and an index" versus "stand up a new service."

Two things actually fork the design:

- **Guardrail alerts vs. streak alerts aren't the same shape.** `quota_exceeded`, `floor_at_risk`, `floor_unreachable`, `config_invalid` map directly to whichever guardrail matched this cycle. But `feed_stale` past 3 cycles, cap pinned 2 cycles, and pace error >15% for 2 cycles need memory across cycles, and `govern()` has none except what's in the persisted state. So those need counters (`stale_cycles`, `pinned_cycles`, `pace_error_cycles`) added to the controller state, incremented/reset inside `govern()`, with the alert surfacing once a counter crosses its threshold. This is also consistent with the fallback rule already implying a stale-cycle counter exists in state.
- **Heartbeat-missed can't be detected inside `govern()` at all** — if the loop didn't run, nothing inside the loop can raise it. That one needs a dead-man's-switch outside the governor: each successful cycle stamps a last-run time per tenant, and a separate watchdog process alerts when that stamp goes stale.

Left at the next level of depth: alert delivery/routing (page vs. log vs. Slack) and whether an alert re-fires every cycle a condition holds or only on transition — SPEC.md doesn't say, and that decision is where dedup logic would go.

Logging from inside route handlers (e.g. `routes/accounts.js`, `routes/orders.js`) only covers writes that remember to call it.

The one wrinkle: triggers only see the DB session, not `req.user`. For "what changed," `old_row`/`new_row` as jsonb (via `to_jsonb(OLD)`/`to_jsonb(NEW)`) is enough for a diff view without a bespoke schema per table, and it scales to new tables by attaching the same trigger function rather than writing new logging code each time.

If stale-after-edit is unacceptable, you instead need the admin tool to purge the CDN by slug on save — real infrastructure, not just a header.

2. **Does `stock` ride inside the cached page, or come out?** `relatedProducts` (~600ms, the dominant cost) and `productBySlug` change at catalogue-edit cadence, but `stockFor` (~250ms) changes on every sale — caching it at the same TTL as the rest of the page risks showing "in stock" after a sellout. Left out: whether that stock split is a second HTTP call from the client or a server-side fragment cache, and any app-level (Redis) cache — not needed here since the CDN is already positioned to do this for free once headers stop blocking it.

- Fixed window (`INCR key; EXPIRE key` per client per minute) is simplest but lets a client burst 2x the limit across a window boundary — exactly the "hammering" pattern you're trying to stop.
- Token bucket (capacity + refill rate, applied via a Lua script for atomicity across concurrent workers) caps sustained rate while still absorbing short legitimate bursts, and one Redis round-trip via `EVAL` avoids a race between workers incrementing concurrently.

Given the symptom (sustained hammering, not just spiky bursts), token bucket is the better fit. Reject with `429` + `Retry-After` before the query runs, using the `plan` column you already select in the auth query to pick limits per tier.

Left out: whether limits should differ per route (`GET /reports` vs `POST /reports`), and what happens to in-flight requests when Redis itself is slow/down (fail-open vs fail-closed) — both are policy calls, not architecture forks.

That eliminates WebSockets, SSE, and long-polling; none can stay open long enough or maintain state to notify a client.

Polling every 5-10s buys nothing but extra invocations; polling every 20-30s catches each update within half a minute of it landing, which is the honest bound here — sub-minute freshness isn't achievable without changing the ingest schedule, which the doc says isn't on the table. Aligning polls to `:00` is a refinement, not a requirement, since clock skew and job-start jitter make exact sync unreliable anyway.

The current code (`payments.js`, `routes/checkout.js`) has no retry and no idempotency key, and `PROVIDER.md` says a timeout from Cardstream means **unknown**, not failed — retrying blind risks a double charge. That's the whole design problem: retrying is only safe once you're sending an `Idempotency-Key`.

The two decisions that actually fork the design:

1. **Idempotency key lifecycle** — generate one key per order pay-attempt and persist it (on the `orders` row or a new `payment_attempts` table) *before* the first request goes out, not in-memory inside `charge()`. Every retry for that attempt reuses the same key; a new customer-initiated attempt gets a new one. This is what turns "timeout, retry" from dangerous into safe — Cardstream will return the original charge, not authorize twice.

2. **What counts as retryable** — only retry on transport failures (the `timeout` event, `req.on("error")`, 5xx). A 4xx from Cardstream is a real decline and must not retry, key or no key.

Everything else is mechanical from there: 2-3 attempts with short exponential backoff inside `charge()`, still bounded well under whatever the customer's waiting on. If all retries exhaust, that's still "unknown," not "failed" — the order shouldn't go back to `pending` (invites a second unkeyed attempt) or show "payment failed" (may have actually succeeded). It needs its own state, e.g. `payment_unknown`, resolved by a reconciliation path — re-querying Cardstream with the same idempotency key, or a webhook — before the customer is told anything definitive.

Depends on scale and how fuzzy the matching needs to be — what's the product catalog size, and roughly what's the write volume (how often do products change)?

Default recommendation: Postgres full-text search (`tsvector`/`tsquery` on name+description, GIN index) plus `pg_trgm` for typo tolerance and partial-word matches. It's already in most stacks, handles ranking via `ts_rank`, and comfortably covers catalogs up to a few hundred thousand rows with sub-50ms queries.

The one fork that matters: stay in Postgres, or reach for a dedicated engine (Typesense/Meilisearch/Elasticsearch). Pick the dedicated engine only if you need instant-as-you-type latency at high query volume, typo-tolerant fuzzy ranking out of the box, or faceted filtering alongside search — that buys you a synced index you have to keep consistent with the product table (via a job or CDC), which is real operational cost the Postgres route avoids.

The pieces are already half-built for this: `storage.js` mints signed S3 URLs but only ever uses `GET`; the comment even flags that presigned `PUT` works with the same credentials and CORS is already open for it. That's the answer — sellers' phones should PUT bytes straight to S3, not through the app.

The fork that matters: **where do the bytes go**. Routing an upload through the storefront (`routes/listings.js` → nginx → app server) hits `client_max_body_size 1m` in `nginx.conf`, and that limit is shared with the payments listener and explicitly frozen for PCI reasons — raising it or carving a per-location exception isn't on the table. A phone camera photo is routinely 3–10MB, so that path is dead before you write a line of code. Presigned `PUT` bypasses the proxy entirely: the seller's browser gets a signed URL from the app, then uploads directly to the bucket, so nginx's cap never applies.

Second fork: **how the app learns the upload happened**, since S3 doesn't tell it. Simplest fit for this codebase: after the PUT succeeds client-side, the browser calls a new endpoint (e.g. `POST /:id/photos { key }`) that does a `HeadObject` to confirm the object actually exists before calling `db.addPhotoKey` — don't trust a client-reported key blindly. The alternative, S3 event notifications into a queue that populates `photo_keys` server-side, avoids trusting the client but adds infra (SQS/Lambda) this project doesn't have yet.

Left out at this depth: constraining the presigned PUT (content-type/size conditions so it can't be abused as an open upload endpoint), HEIC-from-iPhone handling, and thumbnailing — those are next-level-down once the two forks above are settled.

Building on the existing pattern (`if result.guardrail == "quota_exceeded": alert(...)` at line 31-32), most of the eight conditions map directly onto the per-cycle record the supervisor already produces:

- `quota_exceeded`, `floor_at_risk`, `floor_unreachable`, `config_invalid` are single-cycle guardrail values — alert immediately when `result.guardrail` matches, same as the existing example.
- `feed_stale` past three cycles, cap pinned at a band edge for two cycles, and pace error above 15% for two cycles are multi-cycle conditions. Since `govern()` must stay pure for the simulation harness (line 41-42), don't put this counting inside `govern()` itself — track it as a second pure function, `evaluate_alerts(recent_cycles, result)`, that the supervisor calls after `govern()` with a short rolling window of persisted cycle records. It stays testable at simulation speed the same way `govern()` is, and the supervisor is still the only thing doing I/O when it fires `alert(...)`.

The one condition that doesn't fit this shape is **heartbeat missed** — there's no cycle record to inspect because the loop didn't run. That has to be an external watchdog (cron or monitoring check) comparing each tenant's last-persisted-cycle timestamp against "five minutes plus slack," independent of the supervisor process.

So: two pure functions (`govern`, `evaluate_alerts`) feeding one I/O boundary in the supervisor, plus one out-of-band watchdog for the missed-loop case.

Your service already has one choke point for every write: `db.write()` in db.js:13, and `req.user` is resolved for every request in auth.js:5 before any route runs. I'd hang the audit trail there rather than adding logging calls to each route — routes/orders.js and routes/accounts.js don't pass user context into `db.write()` today, and if logging lived in route handlers, the next new write is one missed line away from being unaudited.

**Approach: Postgres triggers + a transaction-scoped actor variable, not app-level log calls.**

1. Pass the actor through the transaction, not through SQL params. Change `db.write(text, params)` to `db.write(text, params, userId)`, and right after `BEGIN` run `SELECT set_config('app.actor_id', $1, true)` with `req.user.id`. The `true` makes it transaction-local — it's gone after COMMIT/ROLLBACK, so concurrent connections never see each other's actor.
2. One generic trigger function, attached to every audited table (`accounts`, `orders`, ...), fired `AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE`. It reads `current_setting('app.actor_id', true)` and inserts a row into `audit_log` with table name, row id, action, actor, `now()`, and `row_to_json(OLD)` / `row_to_json(NEW)` for the diff. This also means the soft-delete pattern in routes/accounts.js:15 (`UPDATE ... SET deleted_at`) is captured automatically as an UPDATE — no special-casing.
3. Lock `audit_log` down: no `UPDATE`/`DELETE` grant for the app's role, so it's append-only. That's what makes it hold up as a compliance artifact rather than just a debug log — the app itself can't rewrite history.

This makes the trail structural (a trigger fires on every write to an audited table, regardless of which code path produced it) instead of relying on every future PR remembering to call a logging function.

Left out, as policy calls rather than architecture: retention/archival for `audit_log`, whether reads need auditing too (compliance asked about writes), and how auditors query this (a read-only view or export job on top of `audit_log`).

Cache-aside at the data layer: store the assembled product record in Redis keyed by product ID (plus locale/currency if the page varies by those), TTL in the minutes range as a backstop, and invalidate explicitly when the product is written rather than waiting out the TTL — otherwise editors see stale prices/descriptions for however long the TTL runs. That alone should take the 900ms down to whatever your app-layer assembly costs, typically single-digit ms on a cache hit.

The fork I can't resolve without knowing more: are these pages personalized or inventory-volatile per request (per-user pricing, live stock counts)? If not, you can go further and cache full rendered pages at a CDN/edge layer, which beats any origin-side cache. If they are, edge caching doesn't work and you're stuck with the data-layer cache above, needing to fetch/render the personalized parts per request.

Add it as middleware in `routes/api.js`, right after the existing auth middleware — that's the earliest point `req.client.client_id` is known, and it has to key on `client_id`, not IP: the code's own comment notes clients share NAT'd addresses and one client can call from many, so IP-based limiting would either miss the offender or throttle innocent bystanders.
