Left out: exact window/limit tuning per plan, and whether boundary bursting (fixed-window's classic weakness) matters enough here to justify a token-bucket instead.

Server push is off the table here, not by choice: WebSocket handshakes 501 at the edge, functions are frozen between invocations, and there's no sticky routing to keep a subscription alive even if one wasn't. So this has to be polling.

The good news is polling fits the data: `rollup` only changes once a minute (jobs/rollup.md), so there's no benefit chasing sub-second freshness. Replace the click-only `load()` in `public/dashboard.js` with a `setInterval` on the same function, at say 15-20s — frequent enough to feel live, well under the 10s function budget per call, and cheap given the endpoint's already 4KB/30ms. Two refinements worth doing at the same time since they're nearly free:

- Skip the re-render when `computed_at` hasn't changed from the last poll, so the UI doesn't flicker/reflow every cycle for no reason.
- Pause the interval on `document.hidden` (Page Visibility API) and resume on visibilitychange, so backgrounded tabs stop generating invocations against the DB.

Everything server-side (`api/metrics.js`, `db.js`) stays as-is — `Cache-Control: no-store` is already correct for this.

The real bug isn't "missing retries" — it's that `payments.js` never sends an `Idempotency-Key`, so `charge()` in `routes/checkout.js` can't safely retry: a timeout per `PROVIDER.md` means the charge state is **unknown**, not failed, and a naive retry risks double-charging the customer.

Fix: generate one idempotency key per order (e.g. the order id, since one order maps to one charge) and send it on the original attempt and every retry. Cardstream then returns the original charge on a retry of a request that actually succeeded, instead of authorizing again.

Two decisions that actually fork the design:

1. **Where the retry happens.** Inline in the request handler (retry once or twice with backoff before responding) is simplest and fine given "a few times a day" is rare — but it makes the customer wait longer per attempt. A background job (mark the order `processing`, return immediately, resolve via a retry worker or a status-check poll) is more resilient and better UX, at the cost of async plumbing and a "processing" state in the UI.
2. **What happens when retries are exhausted and the outcome is still unknown.** Don't collapse that into "failed" — that's the exact bug you're fixing. Either keep the order in a reconciling state and re-check later (Cardstream doesn't have a webhook mentioned in the doc, so this would mean polling `GET` on the charge, if that endpoint exists), or surface "processing" to the customer instead of a false failure.

Given the volume described, I'd lean toward option 1 (inline, 1-2 retries with the idempotency key) plus leaving orders that still fail in a `payment_unknown` status rather than `failed`, with a reconciliation job to clean those up — but that's the depth worth confirming before building.

Recommendation: index product name + description in a proper text-search engine rather than `LIKE` queries, with matching kept tolerant of prefixes/typos since users type "a few words," not exact titles. For a catalog in the thousands, Postgres (`tsvector` + `pg_trgm`) is enough and avoids a new service; past roughly 100k–1M products or once you need relevance ranking/typo tolerance/faceting, a dedicated engine (Meilisearch, Typesense, or OpenSearch) pays for itself. Keep the index updated via a write-through hook on product create/update rather than nightly batch, so new listings are searchable immediately.

The fork I can't resolve without knowing your stack: what's the current catalog size and where does product data live today (Postgres, something else)? That decides which of the two paths above you're actually building.

Direct-to-storage upload with a presigned URL, not proxied through your app server — phone photos run 3-15MB, and round-tripping that through your backend just to forward it to S3/GCS/etc. wastes bandwidth and server memory for no benefit. Flow: app server issues a short-lived presigned PUT URL scoped to the listing, client uploads straight to the bucket, then confirms back to the server (or a bucket event triggers it) to attach the photo record to the listing and kick off thumbnail generation as a background job.

Two things worth doing client-side before the upload fires: downscale/compress via canvas (phone cameras are way bigger than any listing needs to display) and read EXIF orientation so the image isn't sideways — fix both before the bytes leave the device rather than after.

The fork I can't resolve without knowing your stack: which object storage/CDN you're already using, since that determines the presigned-URL mechanism and who generates thumbnails (Lambda/Cloud Function on upload vs a queue worker). What are you running there?

Two places drive this: the `alert(...)` call in the pseudocode (§Control loop) and the list of eight conditions in §Observability, three of which — stale cycles, pinned cap, pace error — require watching consecutive cycles, not just one.

The core fork is where that streak state lives. `govern()` is pure and already tracks "three consecutive stale cycles" internally to decide the fallback-to-default guardrail, so the natural move is to extend its persisted `state` with sibling counters (`cap_pinned_cycles`, `pace_error_cycles`) and have `govern()` emit a separate `alerts: []` list alongside `guardrail` — since alerts and guardrails aren't the same set (cap-pinned and pace-error never change the cap, so they're not guardrails, just diagnostics). The alternative — a stateful alerting layer bolted onto the supervisor, tracking its own history outside the pure core — works too, but duplicates logic `govern()` already has and, more importantly, makes alerts unreproducible by the simulation harness, which replays recorded days specifically because the core has no I/O. Keeping alerts as a pure function of state+inputs means the harness can assert "this shadow week fires these alerts" the same way it asserts caps.

The one condition that can't fit this model is "heartbeat missed" — the loop can't alert on its own absence. That needs an external dead-man's-switch: each successful cycle writes a per-tenant last-run timestamp, and a separate watchdog (cron check, or a Prometheus-style `absent()`/staleness rule) fires when that timestamp goes stale.

Last decision: delivery should be edge-triggered, not level-triggered. `quota_exceeded` holds the cap at zero for the rest of the day — alerting on every 5-minute cycle while that's true would page every 5 minutes until midnight. Fire on transition into the condition, with the supervisor doing dedup/routing at the I/O edge (same place `apply_cap`/`persist_state` already live), not inside `govern()`.

The natural choke point is already there: every write in this service goes through `db.write()` in `db.js:13`, which wraps each call in its own `BEGIN`/`COMMIT`. Extend that one function to take an actor and emit an audit row in the same transaction as the write it's auditing — so the audit entry can never be committed without the write, or vice versa.

Shape:
- `write(text, params, actor)` inserts into `audit_log(occurred_at, actor_id, actor_email, table_name, row_id, action, after)` right after the primary query, using the same client/transaction. `occurred_at` should be the DB clock (`now()`), not app time. `after` comes straight from the existing `RETURNING *`.
- Callers pass `req.user` as the actor. Right now `accounts.js:7` and `accounts.js:15` don't pass any actor at all, and `orders.js:16` cancel doesn't either — those call sites all need updating for this to actually cover "every write," not just new ones.

The fork that matters: **DB triggers vs. this app-level approach.** Triggers are more tamper-resistant (they fire even if a script bypasses the app), but they can't see "who" — this service uses one shared `pg.Pool` with a single DB role, so a trigger only knows the DB user, not `req.user`, unless the app first does `SET LOCAL app.user_id = ...` per request. That's the same plumbing cost as just logging in `db.write()` directly, so given this pooled setup, app-level is the simpler choice for the same guarantee.

Left for the next pass: capturing before-state (needs a `SELECT` before the write, since `RETURNING` only gives you after), making `audit_log` append-only (revoke `UPDATE`/`DELETE` grants for the app role), and who can read the audit table.

Cache-aside with Redis, keyed by product ID, storing the fully assembled product payload (not raw rows) so a hit skips the DB entirely. Two things actually fork the design:

- **Invalidation**: TTL-only (simple, but stale data for up to N seconds) vs. event-based (invalidate/update the key on product write, near-zero staleness but requires wiring cache invalidation into every write path). For product pages, I'd do both — a longer TTL (minutes) as a safety net plus explicit invalidation on writes.
- **Stampede protection**: since these are read-heavy pages, a popular product's cache expiring can trigger a thundering herd of concurrent DB hits. Worth locking/single-flighting the rebuild (or using a short "soft TTL + background refresh") rather than letting every request race to repopulate.

Left out: CDN/edge caching for anonymous traffic, cache warming on deploy, and multi-region consistency — only relevant if traffic or infra scale calls for it.

Key by `client_id`, not IP — the auth middleware in `routes/api.js` already resolves it from the API key, and IP won't work here since one client calls from many addresses and several clients share an address behind the same NAT. State has to live in the existing shared Redis (`redis.js`), not in-process, since `app.js` clusters 4 workers per box with separate heaps and nothing in module scope is shared between them.

Two decisions actually fork the design:

1. **Algorithm.** A Redis `INCR`+`EXPIRE` fixed-window counter per `client_id` is the simplest thing that stops sustained hammering, but it lets a client burst up to 2x the limit right across a window boundary. If the abusive client is bursty at edges rather than just sustained, use a sliding-window (sorted set) or token-bucket (Lua script for atomicity) instead — same Redis, more work per request.
2. **Placement.** Do the check inside the existing `router.use` middleware in `routes/api.js`, right after `req.client` is set and before any `db.query` call. A rejected request should cost one Redis round trip, not a Postgres hit — otherwise the DB is still the thing getting hammered.

Left out: what to do when Redis itself is slow or down — fail open re-admits the hammering client, fail closed takes out every client. Also, `plan` is already sitting on `req.client`, so per-plan limits are a one-line lookup away if you want tiers rather than one global limit.

Push is off the table here: `PLATFORM.md` says WebSocket upgrades 501 at the edge, and functions freeze between invocations, so nothing can hold a connection open to notify clients — SSE dies for the same reason. That leaves polling.

Recommendation: add a `setInterval` around the existing `load()` in `public/dashboard.js`, and skip the re-render when `computed_at` hasn't changed. `/api/metrics` is already cheap (30ms, 4KB, `no-store`), so hitting it on a timer costs nothing extra server-side.

The one real fork is interval length. `rollup` only changes once a minute (`jobs/rollup.md`), so polling faster than ~20-30s buys no fresher data, just more requests — pick something in that range rather than trying to sync to the exact minute boundary (the job's actual run time relative to the client's clock isn't guaranteed).

Left out: pausing the timer on `visibilitychange` when the tab isn't active, and backoff on a failed fetch — worth adding but secondary to the polling loop itself.

The real problem isn't the retry itself, it's that a timeout means you don't know if the charge went through — retrying blindly risks a double charge, and labeling it "failed" is often just wrong.

Two decisions actually fork this:

1. **Idempotency key.** Generate one per checkout attempt and send it on every retry, including automatic ones. Your payment provider dedupes on that key server-side, so a retry after a timeout is safe even if the original charge actually succeeded — it returns the original result instead of charging again.
2. **Where the retry lives.** Either a couple of quick synchronous retries inside the request (simple, but the customer sits there waiting on a flaky network), or move to an async job with backoff: mark the charge "pending" instead of "failed" on timeout, retry a few times off the request path, then resolve via webhook/poll to success or a real failure. Given the symptom you described — timeouts get shown as "failed" — the async version is the fix, since it removes the mislabeling, not just the retries.

Either way, only retry on timeouts/5xx/network errors — never on a card decline or other definitive rejection.

Left out: exact backoff schedule and attempt cap, job queue choice, and the webhook reconciliation logic — that's the next layer down once the approach is picked.

For "a few words" against name/description, the recommendation is Postgres full-text search (or SQLite FTS5) over a dedicated engine — a `tsvector` column with a GIN index, generated from name + description, ranked with `ts_rank`. It's one migration, no new infrastructure, and handles typical prefix/keyword queries fine.

The fork that actually matters: catalog size and quality bar. Under ~100k products, Postgres FTS is plenty and keeps ops simple. If you need typo-tolerance, instant-as-you-type latency, or faceted filtering, that pushes you to Meilisearch or Typesense (still cheap to run) rather than Postgres tricks. Elasticsearch/OpenSearch is worth it only past that, when you also need aggregations at scale — heavier ops cost most teams don't need for name+description search.

Left out: ranking tuning (weighting name over description, recency/popularity boosts) and indexing pipeline (sync on write vs. batch reindex) — those are next-level-down decisions once the engine choice is picked.

Presigned direct-to-storage upload: client requests a signed URL from your backend, uploads the file straight to S3/GCS/Blob, then confirms completion so the backend records the photo against the listing. Proxying multi-MB phone photos through your app server just to relay them to storage wastes request threads and memory for no benefit.

Two decisions actually fork this:

- **Client-side resize before upload vs. accept raw and process server-side.** Phone shots can be 5-15MB HEIC/JPEG. Resizing/compressing in the browser (Canvas API, or a HEIC-to-JPEG conversion step) cuts upload time and mobile data use, but adds client complexity and inconsistent output across devices/browsers. Simpler default: accept raw, cap file size (~20MB) and type client-side, then generate display/thumbnail variants server-side after upload.
- **Sync vs. async variant generation.** Once the original lands in storage, generating thumbnails/resized variants should happen via a background job (storage event trigger or queue), not inline in the request — otherwise the upload confirmation blocks on image processing. Listing photo rows get a status (`pending`/`ready`/`failed`) so the UI can show a placeholder until variants exist.

Left out: moderation/content scanning, CDN delivery config, resumable/chunked upload for flaky mobile connections, and photo ordering/reordering UI — each is a next-level-down detail once the two forks above are picked.

Two layers, not one, because `govern()` can't see its own absence:

**Per-cycle alerts, inside the pure core.** Most of the eight conditions (`quota_exceeded`, `feed_stale` past 3 cycles, cap pinned 2 cycles, pace error >15% for 2 cycles, `floor_at_risk`, `floor_unreachable`, `config_invalid`) are all derivable from `state` + `inputs`, the same inputs `govern()` already takes. So extend `govern()`'s return to a list of alert signals alongside the single `guardrail` field, and have the supervisor dispatch that list to an alert sink after persisting state — same pattern as the existing `if result.guardrail == "quota_exceeded": alert(...)` line, just generalized. This keeps alert logic inside the pure core, so it's covered by the same unit tests and simulation harness instead of being untestable side-effect code bolted onto the loop.

**Heartbeat missed, outside it.** This is the one condition `govern()` structurally cannot produce — it only fires when the loop runs, and this alert fires when it doesn't. That needs a separate watchdog reading the persisted "last cycle" timestamp per tenant and firing when it's stale beyond ~2x the 5-minute interval. It's not part of the control loop at all.

The fork worth resolving before building: "cap pinned for two cycles" and "pace error >15% for two cycles" require consecutive-cycle counters, and today only `feed_stale` carries one in state. You'd add two more counters to persisted state, mirroring that existing pattern. The other thing left unspecified is dedup/throttle policy — alerting every cycle while a condition holds vs. only on transition edges — which the doc doesn't address and you'd need to decide before wiring a real sink.

Since `db.write()` is already the single chokepoint every write goes through, and every request already carries `req.user` from the `sessionUser` middleware, I'd anchor the audit trail there rather than instrumenting each route in `routes/accounts.js` / `routes/orders.js` individually.

- **`audit_log` table**: `id, table_name, row_id, action, actor_id, changed_at default now(), old_row jsonb, new_row jsonb`.
- **Generic trigger** on each writable table (`accounts`, `orders`, ...) that fires `AFTER INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE` and inserts into `audit_log` using `row_to_json(OLD)`/`NEW` and `current_setting('app.actor_id', true)` for who. Triggers guarantee coverage even for writes that skip the JS layer later — a migration, a psql session, a route someone forgets to instrument.
- **One change in `db.js`**: at the top of `write()`'s transaction, run `SELECT set_config('app.actor_id', $1, true)` with the caller's user id. The `true` scopes it to the transaction, so it's cleared on commit/rollback and can't bleed across pooled connections. That means `write()`'s signature needs to accept an actor id, and the three call sites in `accounts.js`/`orders.js` need to pass `req.user.id`.

The real fork: DB-level triggers (above) vs. logging inside `db.write()` itself keyed off table/action metadata each caller passes explicitly. The app-level version is less plumbing but only as complete as every future caller remembers to be; triggers hold even when someone forgets — and "for every write" is exactly the guarantee compliance is asking for, so I'd pick triggers.

Left out: locking down `audit_log` itself (revoke `UPDATE`/`DELETE` on it, or ship rows to append-only storage) and how auditors query/export it.

Cache-aside with Redis in front of the DB, keyed by product ID: on a page request, check Redis first; on miss, query the DB, populate the cache with a TTL, and return. That collapses the ~900ms to a few ms on hits and needs no application logic changes beyond wrapping the existing product-fetch calls.

Two things fork the design and I can't resolve them without knowing your data:

1. **Is the page identical for every viewer?** If price/stock/personalization aren't baked into the page, cache the full rendered fragment (or the whole page) — maximum win, one cache entry serves everyone. If price or inventory varies by user/region/warehouse, you can't cache the whole page; cache the slow, shared parts (description, images, reviews, related items) and leave price/stock as live per-request DB calls (they're usually cheap single-row lookups, not the 900ms culprit).

2. **How stale can it be?** TTL alone (e.g. 5–15 min) is simplest and fine if product edits are rare and a short staleness window is acceptable. If editors expect changes to show up immediately, add invalidation on write — bust the cache key when the product record updates — with the TTL kept as a backstop for cases the invalidation path misses.

Recommendation: start with cache-aside + TTL on the static/shared parts of the page, keyed by product ID, and only add write-triggered invalidation if staleness turns out to matter in practice — it's extra moving parts you don't need on day one.

Per-client token bucket, keyed by API key/client ID (not IP — one abusive key can sit behind a shared IP, and legitimate multi-user IPs shouldn't get punished for it). Token bucket over fixed/sliding window because it naturally allows short bursts but caps sustained rate, which is exactly the "hammering" pattern you're seeing.

Two things actually fork the design:

1. **Where state lives** — if `/v1` runs on multiple instances, per-process in-memory counters won't catch a client that spreads requests across them; you need a shared store (Redis, `INCR`+`EXPIRE` or a Lua script for atomicity) so the limit holds cluster-wide. Single instance, in-memory is fine and simpler.
2. **Where it's enforced** — at the gateway/edge (nginx, Envoy, API gateway) before requests reach app code, vs. as middleware inside the app. Edge enforcement protects the app's CPU/DB from ever seeing the excess load; app-level middleware is easier to wire to per-client business logic (different tiers/quotas) but the request still costs you a connection and some processing before being rejected.

Given "degrading it for everybody else," I'd default to edge-enforced + Redis-backed unless you tell me it's a single instance — that combination is what actually stops the load rather than just rejecting it late. Rejected requests get `429` with a `Retry-After` header so well-behaved clients back off correctly.

Left out: per-tier limit values, how you detect and communicate with the offending client, and burst-allowance tuning — those are configuration, not architecture.

WebSockets are off the table here — `PLATFORM.md` says connection upgrades 501 at the edge and functions are frozen/killed at 10s, so nothing can hold a push connection open. That leaves polling from `public/dashboard.js`.

Since `rollup` only changes once a minute (`jobs/rollup.md`) and `/api/metrics` already returns `computed_at`, poll on an interval (every 15–20s is plenty against a 1-minute cadence) and skip the re-render when `computed_at` hasn't changed from the last fetch — cheap given the endpoint's already 4KB/30ms, and avoids fighting the DOM on every tick for no reason.

Left out: pausing the poll when the tab is hidden (`visibilitychange`) and a retry/backoff for failed fetches — worth adding but not the core mechanism.

**Approach**, grounded in what's here: `payments.js` sends no `Idempotency-Key`, and `checkout.js` treats a timeout the same as a decline (`catch` -> `502 payment failed`). `PROVIDER.md` says a timeout on this endpoint is genuinely ambiguous — the charge may have gone through — and that replaying the same request with the same idempotency key returns the original result rather than double-charging.

So the fix has three parts:

1. **Generate an idempotency key per order before the first attempt**, store it on the order row, and send it as `Idempotency-Key` on every attempt for that order. This has to be persisted *before* the network call, not derived from the response — otherwise a crash between sending the request and writing the result leaves you with no way to safely replay.
2. **Split the `catch` in `checkout.js` by error type.** A provider timeout is retryable and must not touch `status`; a 4xx (declined, insufficient funds) is a real failure and can map to `payment failed` today. Retry the timed-out call with the *same* key, bounded (e.g. 2–3 attempts, short backoff) — safe because the vendor guarantees the replay is a no-op if the first attempt already authorised.
3. **If retries are exhausted, don't show "failed."** Leave the order in a `payment_pending`/`unknown` status and reconcile later (a periodic sweep that replays the stored key for any order stuck in that state) rather than surfacing a false failure to the customer.

One fork I can't resolve from the code: retrying inline inside the request handler versus moving the charge off the request path into a background job triggered after the pending order + key are saved. Inline is the smaller change and fits the current single-request structure; a background job is more resilient if the app process itself can die mid-request, but is a bigger structural change. Given "a few times a day," I'd start with inline bounded retry plus a periodic reconciliation sweep for the leftovers, and only move to a job queue if the crash-mid-request case turns out to matter in practice.

Postgres full-text search, not a separate search service — 38k rows growing by a few hundred a month doesn't justify standing up Elasticsearch/Algolia/Meilisearch. Concretely: add a generated `tsvector` column on `products` combining `name` and `description` (weighted, name higher), a GIN index on it, then a new `GET /search?q=` route in `routes/products.js` following the existing `db.query` pattern, using `websearch_to_tsquery` and ranking by `ts_rank`.

The fork worth deciding: plain FTS (word-based, stemmed) handles "wireless keyboard" fine but won't match typos or partial words like "keybrd" — if that matters for your users, layer in `pg_trgm` similarity as a fallback or combine it with FTS in the ranking. That's the depth I'd leave for implementation, not decide now.

Direct-to-storage upload: the backend issues a presigned upload URL (S3/GCS/etc.), the phone uploads the binary straight to blob storage, then pings the backend to create the photo record and attach it to the listing. Keeps large binaries off your app servers.

Compress client-side before upload: phone photos run 3-12MB and iPhones default to HEIC. Downscale to ~2048px on the longest edge and re-encode to JPEG on-device before uploading — cuts upload time on mobile data and sidesteps HEIC-support gaps downstream.

After the backend confirms the upload, an async worker should strip EXIF GPS data (sellers photographing from home) and generate thumbnail/display-size variants, served via CDN.

The fork: presigned direct-to-storage vs. proxying the upload through your own server. Direct is the standard choice unless you need synchronous server-side validation (moderation, fraud checks) before accepting the file — that forces a proxy. Which storage/backend are you on? That decides the presigned-URL mechanics. Left out: resumable/chunked upload for flaky mobile connections (multipart or tus) — worth adding once basic upload works.

Two condition types show up in the Observability section, and they don't map onto the architecture the same way.

**Straightforward ones** — `quota_exceeded`, `floor_at_risk`, `floor_unreachable`, `config_invalid` — are just `result.guardrail` values, same as the `alert("quota exceeded", tenant)` line already in the pseudocode. Trivial: `if result.guardrail == X: alert(...)`.

**The forking decisions:**

1. Four conditions aren't single-cycle checks — `feed_stale` past 3 cycles, cap pinned 2 consecutive cycles, pace error >15% for 2 consecutive cycles. Since `govern()` is pure and stateless between calls except via `state`, that streak-counting has to live in the persisted `state`/`result` — not bolted onto the supervisor — or the simulation harness stops being able to exercise alerting deterministically at replay speed. This mirrors how `feed_stale`'s existing 3-cycle-to-fallback logic already works; extend the same pattern to carry a `cap_clamped` streak and a computed pace-error streak, and have `govern()` return which alerts are newly due each cycle.

2. Heartbeat-missed can't be produced by the loop at all — a missed heartbeat means the loop didn't run, so nothing inside it can detect its own absence. That needs an external watchdog: something scheduled independently that checks, per tenant, whether a cycle-completion timestamp landed within the expected 5-minute window, and pages if not.

Left out: alert routing/severity/dedup (who gets paged vs. logged), and who watches the watchdog.

Every write in this service already funnels through one place: `db.write()` in `db.js` — it's the sole transaction boundary, called by every route (`accounts.js`, `orders.js`). That choke point is where to hook the audit trail, not each route handler individually, so no future route can forget to log.

**Design:**
- Add an `audit_log` table: `id, table_name, row_id, action, actor_id, actor_email, diff jsonb, occurred_at`.
- Populate it with `AFTER INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE` triggers on `accounts` and `orders` (and any table added later) that write `OLD`/`NEW` as jsonb into `audit_log`. Triggers are generic — one trigger function, applied per table — and can't be bypassed by a route that forgets to call a logging helper, or by a write issued outside the app (a migration, a manual `psql` fix).
- The gap: triggers run inside Postgres and can't see `req.user`. Fix it at the one place that already opens every write transaction — have `write()` run `SET LOCAL app.actor_id = $1` (and `app.actor_email`) using `req.user`, which `sessionUser` in `auth.js` has already resolved before any route handler runs. The trigger reads `current_setting('app.actor_id')` into the audit row. This needs `write()`'s signature to accept an actor, and every call site (`accounts.js`, `orders.js`) to pass `req.user` through — the one change that touches existing code, but it's mechanical.

**The fork:** DB triggers vs. logging inside `write()` in JS. Triggers win here because `write()` only receives raw SQL text and params — it doesn't generically know the table/row being touched unless you parse the SQL (fragile) or make every call site pass `{table, action}` explicitly (easy to forget, same problem triggers solve). Triggers read `OLD`/`NEW` directly from the row Postgres already has.

**Left for the next level down:** the trigger function itself (one generic `row_to_jsonb(OLD)`/`row_to_jsonb(NEW)` function reused per table via `CREATE TRIGGER ... EXECUTE FUNCTION`), making `audit_log` append-only (revoke `UPDATE`/`DELETE` grants from the app's DB role), and retention/export policy for whatever compliance actually queries against.

**Recommendation:** Cache-aside with Redis in front of the DB read, keyed by product ID (`product:{id}`), short TTL (e.g. 60s) as a backstop, plus explicit invalidation on writes.

Two decisions actually fork the design:

**Is the page identical for every visitor?** If yes (no per-account pricing/inventory), also cache the rendered page at the CDN/edge with purge-on-publish — that skips your app entirely for the common case and is the bigger win than Redis alone. If it's personalized, skip the CDN and keep caching at the data layer only.

**How do writes happen?** If product updates go through one service, invalidate the key synchronously on write — deterministic freshness, no stale reads. If updates come from multiple paths (admin UI, bulk import, migrations), chasing every write site isn't worth it — lean on the short TTL instead and skip explicit invalidation.

Left out: stampede protection (locking so an expiring hot key doesn't send N concurrent requests to the DB) and hit-rate monitoring — add those once it's live and you can see real traffic against it.

Key on `client_id`, not IP — `routes/api.js:9-19` shows clients share NAT and call from multiple addresses, so IP would both under-block the offender and over-block their neighbors. The auth middleware already resolves `req.client.client_id` (and `plan`) before any handler runs, so that's the natural point to check a counter.

Store the counter in the existing Redis (`redis.js`) rather than in-process: `app.js` runs 4 cluster workers per box with nothing shared between them, and Redis is already "the only piece of state the workers have in common." A per-worker counter would let a client blow through 4x the intended limit just by hitting different workers.

Two decisions actually fork the design:

1. **Fixed window vs. sliding window/token bucket.** Fixed window is one `INCR` + `PEXPIRE` on a key like `ratelimit:{client_id}:{minute}` — cheap, one round trip, good enough to stop a client from hammering everyone else. Sliding window/token bucket is smoother (no edge-of-window burst) but needs a Lua script for atomicity. For "stop one client from degrading it for everybody," fixed window is enough.
2. **One bucket per client for all of `/v1`, or per-route.** `POST /reports` writes to Postgres, `GET /reports` just reads; a write-heavy abuser doesn't need to also eat the read quota. A single bucket is simpler and fixes the immediate problem; per-route buckets cost one extra Redis key per route.

Enforce it as middleware placed right after the auth middleware in `routes/api.js`, so a limited request gets a `429` (with `Retry-After`) before it ever reaches `db.query`. Since `req.client.plan` is already available, the limit can vary by plan without an extra lookup.

Left out: actual limit numbers per plan, and whether repeated violations should escalate to a longer ban/API-key throttle — that's a policy call, not an architecture one.

The platform rules out the fancy options: WebSocket upgrades 501 at the edge, and functions freeze between invocations, so no SSE or push either — nothing can hold a connection open or notify the client on its own.

That leaves polling, and the rollup job caps how useful faster polling would be anyway: `rollup` only changes once a minute, on the minute, written by the one scheduled job. So poll `/api/metrics` on an interval slightly over 60s (e.g. every 65s, or align to the minute boundary) and skip the re-render when `computed_at` hasn't changed from the last fetch — `dashboard.js` already reads `computed_at`, so that's just comparing it before calling `render()` instead of always rendering. Polling faster than 60s would just hammer the endpoint for identical rows.

If a browser tab needs to be more responsive right when the minute rolls over, jitter is the only refinement worth adding (each client offsets its poll slightly so they don't all hit `/api/metrics` in the same instant) — not a fundamentally different transport, since the platform doc says moving off it isn't happening.

The provider doc (`PROVIDER.md`) spells out the actual bug: a Cardstream timeout means *unknown*, not failed, and `checkout.js` currently maps every exception — including timeout — straight to `"payment failed"`. Retrying isn't really the hard part; making retries *safe* is, and that hinges on the `Idempotency-Key` header the code never sends.

**Core mechanism:** generate one idempotency key per payment attempt and persist it on the order *before* the first `charge()` call goes out (e.g. an `idempotency_key` column set at the top of the route, in the same transaction as reading the order). Every retry of that order — automatic or the customer clicking "pay" again after seeing a failure — must resend that same stored key, never a fresh one. That's what turns a second charge call into "give me the result of the first one" instead of a second authorization.

Two decisions actually fork the design from there:

1. **Inline vs. async retry.** Given a 10s provider timeout, a bounded inline retry (1–2 extra attempts with the same key, short backoff) fits the current synchronous handler with the least change in shape. It only breaks down if Cardstream's slowness is correlated (the retry times out too) — in which case you want to return "processing" immediately, retry from a background job, and resolve the order via poll or webhook instead of holding the HTTP request open.
2. **What "still unresolved after retries" means.** Per the vendor's own guidance, exhausting retries should not fall back to `"payment failed"` — it should land the order in a distinct `pending`/`unknown` state and hand off to a reconciliation path (a job that re-queries or retries later with the same key), since a real decline and an unresolved timeout are different customer-facing and financial situations.

Everything else — backoff curve, retry count, queue choice — is detail underneath those two calls.

At 38k rows on Postgres 16, this is a Postgres full-text search job — no need for Elasticsearch/Meilisearch.

Add a generated `tsvector` column on `products` combining `name` and `description` with `name` weighted higher (`setweight(..., 'A')` vs `'B'`), back it with a GIN index, then add a `GET /search?q=` route that runs `websearch_to_tsquery('english', q)` against it and orders by `ts_rank`. `websearch_to_tsquery` is the right parser here since it takes raw user-typed phrases (handles quotes, `-exclude`, multiple words) rather than requiring `&`/`|` syntax.

Two decisions actually fork the design:
- **Stemmed full-text vs. substring/prefix matching.** FTS gives relevance ranking and handles plurals/word forms, but it won't match mid-word or typo'd fragments (e.g. "wat bottle" typed one letter off gets nothing, and no partial "hood" → "hoodie" while typing). If autocomplete-as-you-type matters, add `pg_trgm` + a trigram GIN index on `name` for prefix/fuzzy matching, used underneath a search-box typeahead, with the tsvector search serving the main results page. If it's just a "hit enter, see results" search box, plain FTS alone is enough.
- **Sync mechanism for the tsvector column.** A `GENERATED ALWAYS AS (...) STORED` column keeps it trivially in sync on insert/update with zero app code, at the cost of a small write penalty — fine at hundreds of writes/month. That's the right call here; a trigger or app-side recompute is unnecessary complexity at this scale.

Direct-to-S3 with presigned PUT, bypassing nginx entirely — the pieces for it already exist and are unused.

The blocker: `nginx.conf` caps `client_max_body_size` at 1m globally, and that's fixed on purpose (PCI scope for the payments listener on the same nginx, per-location override declined). A phone camera photo routinely runs 3-8MB, so any upload proxied through the storefront through this nginx gets rejected before it reaches your app code. Raising the limit isn't on the table.

So the upload can't go storefront to app to S3. It has to go client to S3 directly:

1. Client asks the storefront for a signed PUT URL for a given listing (`storage.js:signedUrl` already supports `method: 'PUT'`, and bucket CORS already allows PUT from `market.example.com` — this was set up for the internal tool and never wired to a route).
2. Client PUTs the photo bytes straight to S3 with that URL. This traffic never touches nginx, so the 1MB cap doesn't apply.
3. Client calls the storefront back with the key to confirm, which calls `db.addPhotoKey` — the column's been sitting there unused since it was added.

That's two small JSON endpoints on the existing `listings` router (request an upload URL, confirm a key), no nginx or payments-service changes, no new infra.

The one thing left to decide: HEIC. iPhones camera-roll photos in HEIC by default, which most browsers can't render. Worth confirming whether the client (app or web) converts to JPEG before the PUT, or whether the listing photo pipeline needs to handle HEIC on read.

Two forks decide this, both visible in the spec itself:

1. **Where alert calls live.** The pseudocode already shows `alert()` called from the supervisor after `govern()` returns, not from inside `govern()` — keep that. `govern()` stays pure (SPEC.md:37-42), so all 8 conditions in the Observability list (SPEC.md:64-73) get evaluated in the supervisor's per-cycle loop, right where `quota_exceeded` already fires one.

2. **Where multi-cycle memory lives.** Most of those conditions aren't single-cycle guardrail matches — `feed_stale` past three cycles, cap pinned for two consecutive cycles, pace error above 15% for two consecutive cycles. Since `govern()` is the only thing carrying persisted state across cycles, the cleanest fit is extending `result.state` with the running consecutive-cycle counters (it already tracks something like this for the three-cycle `feed_stale` fallback in the Guardrails section) so the supervisor's alert check is a stateless lookup on `result`, not a second, parallel piece of state-tracking logic outside the tested core.

The outlier is **heartbeat missed**: it can't be raised from inside the per-tenant loop, because a missed cycle means the loop didn't run at all. That needs an external watchdog — a separate process checking each tenant's last-persisted cycle timestamp against wall clock and firing if it's older than one interval.

Left for the next level down: alert dedup/throttling (so a stuck `quota_exceeded` doesn't page every 5 minutes) and which channel/severity each condition maps to.

Two things funnel every write already: `db.write()` in db.js:13-26 opens one transaction per call, and `sessionUser` in auth.js:5-13 resolves `req.user` for every request. Both are single choke points — build the audit trail off them rather than adding logging to each route.

**Capture "what changed" with Postgres triggers, not app code.** An `AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE` trigger on each audited table, writing `row_to_json(OLD)`/`row_to_json(NEW)` into an `audit_log` table, fires no matter how the row was written — today's routes, a future route someone forgets to instrument, a one-off migration, a psql session. Per-route logging can't make that guarantee; routes/orders.js:14 already shows how easy it is to add a write with nothing extra attached.

**Get "who" into the trigger via the transaction, not the row.** Triggers can't see `req.user`. Have `db.write()` run `SET LOCAL app.actor_id = $1` on the same client before the real query (db.js:14-18 already opens a dedicated client per write, so this is one extra line, no signature change needed at call sites). Source the actor from `req.user` set in auth.js:11 by threading it through Node's `AsyncLocalStorage`, set once in the `sessionUser` middleware — so accounts.js and orders.js don't need to change at all, and neither does any future route. The trigger reads `current_setting('app.actor_id', true)` and falls back to null/"system" for writes that bypass the app (which is itself a useful signal to flag).

Schema: `audit_log(id, table_name, row_pk, operation, actor_id, old_row jsonb, new_row jsonb, occurred_at timestamptz default now())`, indexed on `(table_name, row_pk)` and `(actor_id)` for "who changed what." Revoke UPDATE/DELETE on `audit_log` from the app's DB role so it's append-only — a compromised app account still can't edit its own trail.

Left out at this depth: retention/archival policy, and whether compliance needs the trail exported off this database entirely (object-locked S3, separate audited store) for tamper-resistance beyond revoked grants — worth a follow-up once you know which regime you're satisfying (SOC 2, HIPAA, etc.).

Cache the data layer, not the page: a Redis read-through cache in front of the product query, keyed by product ID (`product:{id}`), with a short TTL (5–15 min) as a safety net and explicit invalidation on writes (product update/inventory change publishes a cache delete). That replaces the 900ms DB round-trip with a sub-millisecond hit on cache, and correctness is enforced by invalidation rather than by waiting out a TTL.

Two decisions actually fork this design:

- **Page-level vs data-level.** If the product page renders identically for every visitor, put a full-page cache in front (CDN/edge or Varnish) — simpler and faster than caching queries. If there's per-user content (cart state, personalized pricing, recommendations), page-level breaks immediately, so cache just the DB results and let the page render around them.
- **TTL-only vs event-driven invalidation.** TTL alone is less code but serves stale prices/inventory for up to the TTL window. Event-driven invalidation stays correct but means every write path that touches product data has to remember to bust the cache.

Left out: stampede protection when a hot key expires (locking or jitter so 1000 requests don't all miss and hit the DB at once), and a warming strategy for the long tail of rarely-viewed products that never gets a cache hit anyway.

Which fits — is the page the same for all visitors, and roughly how many distinct products/write frequency are we talking about?

Key by `req.client.client_id`, not IP — the auth middleware in `routes/api.js` already resolves it, and the comment there is right that IP is useless (shared NAT, multiple addresses per client). Enforce it in Redis, since `redis.js` is the one thing the 4 per-box workers already share (in-process counters would let each worker allow its own separate quota).

Concretely: a small middleware inserted right after the `X-Api-Key` lookup, before the route handlers, that runs an atomic Lua script (`EVAL`) against `redis.js`'s client doing `INCR ratelimit:{client_id}` + `PEXPIRE` on first hit — one round trip, no race between the check and the increment. On limit exceeded, respond `429` with `Retry-After` instead of hitting `db.query`, so Postgres and the route logic never even see the excess load. Since `req.client.plan` is already fetched, the limit itself is a lookup per plan tier rather than one global constant.

The one real fork: fixed-window `INCR`+`EXPIRE` (simple, one edge case where 2x burst can land across a window boundary) vs. a token-bucket Lua script (smooths bursts properly, slightly more code). For "one client hammering it," fixed-window is enough to stop the bleeding; token bucket is the upgrade if bursty-but-compliant clients start getting falsely throttled at the edges.

Left out: what limit/plan values to use, and whether to also cap at the LB/gateway layer as defense-in-depth before requests even reach a worker.

Given the platform constraints in `PLATFORM.md`, this resolves to one option, not really a choice: WebSockets are rejected at the edge (501) and SSE/long-polling both need a connection held open past what a frozen, 10-second serverless invocation can do. That leaves **client-side polling** as the only viable push-like mechanism.

The one thing worth tuning is the interval, since it's the only free variable left. `jobs/rollup.md` says data changes at most once a minute, on the minute, so polling faster than that just adds load for no new data. In `public/dashboard.js`, replace the click-only `load()` with a `setInterval` (something like every 15–20s so the UI catches the new `computed_at` shortly after each minute boundary), and skip the re-render when the fetched `computed_at` hasn't changed from the last one — `api/metrics.js` already returns `computed_at` per response, so that comparison is free.

Left for the next level down: backoff on fetch failure, and pausing the interval via the Page Visibility API when the tab isn't active (each of these is a few lines, not a design fork).

The core issue isn't the retry loop — it's that a timeout is ambiguous. You don't know if the charge actually landed on the processor's side, so blindly retrying risks a double charge, and blindly failing risks losing a sale that already succeeded.

**Recommendation:**

1. Generate one idempotency key per checkout attempt and send it on every retry. Any processor worth using (Stripe, Adyen, etc.) will return the original result instead of charging twice if the same key comes in again.
2. On timeout, don't mark it "failed" yet — mark it "processing" and query the processor for that idempotency key's real status before doing anything else. If it succeeded, complete the order. Only if it's genuinely still unresolved do you retry.
3. Run the retry (with backoff, capped at a few attempts) as a background job, not inline in the request — the customer already waited once for a timeout; a second synchronous wait just risks a second timeout.
4. Keep timeout and decline as separate states in your charge state machine. A decline is terminal and shouldn't retry the same card; a timeout is transient and should.

The one decision that actually forks the design: whether the customer waits on a "processing" screen for the async resolution, or checks out immediately and gets notified (email/webhook to your UI) if the delayed charge fails. That's a UX call tied to your checkout flow, not a payments one.

Direct-to-storage upload, not proxied through your app server: client asks your backend for a presigned URL (S3/GCS/R2) scoped to that listing, PUTs the file straight to the bucket, then tells the backend to attach the resulting object key to the listing. That keeps multi-MB phone photos off your app server's memory/bandwidth.

The other fork is where resizing happens. Do a client-side downscale/compress before upload (canvas or the browser's image APIs, HEIC→JPEG, cap to ~2048px) — phone cameras produce 3-12MB files, and shrinking before upload matters more than after on mobile networks. Then on the backend, trigger thumbnail/variant generation asynchronously off the storage-write event (queue or bucket trigger), not inline in the request, and serve everything through a CDN.

Server side still needs to validate content-type/size and re-check the presigned URL's auth scope — never trust the client's resize or MIME claim.

That's the shape; the depth I'm leaving out is upload progress/retry UX for flaky connections and EXIF orientation handling.

Extend the pure core to track the stateful conditions, and keep the actual alert I/O in the supervisor, matching the existing `quota_exceeded` pattern.

Most of the eight conditions are just per-cycle guardrail results (`floor_at_risk`, `floor_unreachable`, `config_invalid`, `quota_exceeded`) — `govern()` already returns these, so the supervisor can alert on them directly, same as line 31-32.

The three that need cross-cycle memory (`feed_stale` past three cycles, cap pinned two cycles, pace error above 15% two cycles) should be tracked as counters inside `result.state`, since `govern()` already does this for the stale-cycle fallback (line 51-52). Extend that state with `consecutive_pinned` and `consecutive_pace_error` counters, and have `govern()` return which alert conditions are newly true this cycle (e.g. `result.alerts: [...]`) rather than calling `alert()` itself — that keeps the core pure and testable at simulation speed, and the supervisor just fans `result.alerts` out to the alerting sink after `apply_cap`/`persist_state`.

The one condition that can't work this way is "heartbeat missed" — a loop that isn't running can't report its own absence. That needs an external watchdog (separate cron/monitor) that checks the last-persisted cycle timestamp per tenant and fires if it's older than one interval.

The fork you'd need to resolve: does the counter state (`consecutive_pinned`, etc.) live in the same persisted `state` blob `govern()` already owns, or in a separate observability-only store? Keeping it in the same state is simpler and keeps one source of truth, but couples alerting thresholds to the controller's persistence schema and the simulation harness's replay fixtures.

The core pattern: capture the audit event **in the same transaction as the write**, in an **append-only store the app can only insert into**, keyed by actor + entity + timestamp + before/after diff.

Concretely:
- **Where to hook**: intercept at the data-access layer (ORM hook, repository wrapper, or DB trigger) rather than scattering `logAudit()` calls through business logic — otherwise someone adds a new write path and forgets it.
- **What to record per write**: actor id (from auth context, not client-supplied), entity type + id, action (create/update/delete), before/after values (or a diff), timestamp, and a request/trace id for correlation.
- **Atomicity**: write the audit row in the same DB transaction as the mutation, so a failed audit write rolls back the change — no silent gaps.
- **Tamper evidence**: audit table is insert-only (revoke UPDATE/DELETE at the DB permission level), and for stronger compliance guarantees, hash-chain each row (hash of previous row + this row's content) so deletion/edits are detectable.

Two decisions genuinely fork the implementation and depend on your stack:
1. **Capture point** — application-level hook (easy actor context, but only as complete as your discipline) vs. DB-level trigger/CDC (catches every write including raw SQL/migrations, but "who" has to be threaded through as a session variable).
2. **Sync vs async** — write audit rows inline in-transaction (simplest, guarantees no gaps) vs. transactional outbox + stream to a separate immutable store (better if audit volume/retention needs to scale independently of the primary DB).

What's the service's stack and DB — that decides which of those two forks fits.

The bottleneck isn't something a new cache layer needs to be built for — it already exists. `middleware/security.js` applies `Cache-Control: no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate, private` to every route, including `/p`, and `CDN.md` confirms the edge CDN honors exactly that header and nothing else. That's why hit rate is 0%: the app is telling the CDN never to cache anything. The no-store rule was a rushed, blanket fix for a real leak on `/account` (per-user order data), not a requirement of `/p` — the product page is anonymous, identical for every visitor, and the catalog only changes a few times a day via the admin tool.

So the build is: scope that header so it's still forced on `/account`, and give `/p/:slug` its own response header, e.g. `Cache-Control: public, max-age=300, stale-while-revalidate=60`. The CDN then serves repeat requests for a slug straight from the edge — skipping `productBySlug`, `relatedProducts` (the 600ms join), and `stockFor` entirely, not just speeding them up. No Redis, no invalidation plumbing: a multi-minute TTL is fine against "edits a few times a day," and it self-corrects on expiry.

One decision I can't make for you: `stockFor` is baked into that same cached response, so under a public TTL the displayed stock can lag by up to `max-age`. If checkout re-validates stock anyway, that's likely fine and you ship the single cached response. If a stale "in stock" on the page itself is a problem, stock needs to be split out to a separate low-TTL/uncached call the page fetches, and only the shell gets the long TTL.

Rate-limit per client identity (API key, not IP — IPs get shared behind NAT/proxies), using a token bucket keyed by client ID, enforced at the gateway/edge before requests reach `/v1` handlers. Token bucket over fixed windows because it smooths bursts instead of allowing a client to burn its whole quota in the first second of each window, and it's a single counter + timestamp per client rather than a sliding log.

The fork that matters: where the bucket state lives. If `/v1` runs on multiple instances, an in-memory bucket per process lets a client multiply its effective quota by hitting different instances — you need a shared store (Redis `INCR`+`EXPIRE` or a Lua script for atomicity) that all instances check. If it's a single instance, in-memory is fine and simpler.

On limit, return `429` with `Retry-After` rather than silently dropping, so well-behaved clients back off instead of retrying immediately and making it worse.

Left out: the actual limit/burst numbers (depends on `/v1`'s real capacity, which you'd get from load-testing, not guessing), and whether you also want a global circuit breaker on top so a single client can't degrade others even before hitting their own cap — that's a second, coarser limit ahead of the per-client one.

The rollup job (`jobs/rollup.md`) writes fresh data once a minute, on the minute, and it's the only writer — nothing can know sooner than that. `api/metrics.js` is a stateless serverless function already, and `PLATFORM.md` rules out anything that needs a live connection: WebSocket upgrades 501 at the edge, there's no sticky routing, and instances freeze between invocations so a timer or subscription can't outlive one request anyway.

That rules out WebSockets/SSE outright — it has to be the browser polling `/api/metrics` on an interval. The only real fork is cadence: a naive short interval (say every 3-5s) works but multiplies invocations for no benefit, since the data is byte-identical until the top of the minute. Better to poll every 15-20s and compare the returned `computed_at` against what's rendered, skipping the re-render when it hasn't changed — cheap given the response is already 4KB/30ms. Pair it with a `visibilitychange` listener to stop polling when the tab isn't visible, so idle dashboards don't run up invocations for nobody.

Concretely: replace the click-only `load()` in `public/dashboard.js` with `setInterval(load, ...)`, keep the existing `no-store` fetch, and gate the DOM update on `computed_at` changing. The "Refresh" button can stay as a manual force-check or just get deleted.

Left unresolved: exact interval and whether to align polls to `:00` boundaries instead of a flat interval — that's a tradeoff between perceived latency and invocation count that depends on traffic/cost tolerance you'd need to set.

The failure here isn't really "retry needs backoff" — it's that a timeout is ambiguous (you don't know if the gateway actually charged the card), so retrying blindly risks a double charge, and showing "failed" immediately is often just wrong.

Recommended shape:

1. **Idempotency key per charge attempt** (stable per order/invoice, sent to the gateway — Stripe etc. support this natively). Retrying with the same key returns the original result instead of creating a second charge.
2. **On timeout, don't conclude failure** — retry the same idempotent request (or query charge status by that key) and let the gateway tell you what actually happened.
3. **Move off the synchronous request path**: mark the charge `processing`, return that to the customer immediately, and do the retries (exponential backoff + jitter, capped attempts) in a background job. Resolve via the gateway's webhook rather than guessing.
4. **Persist an explicit state machine** (`pending → processing → succeeded/failed`) so the retry job, the webhook, and whatever the customer sees can't race into showing different answers.
5. Only retry transient errors (timeout/network/5xx) — never retry a hard decline.

The one fork worth deciding explicitly: synchronous retry-then-respond vs. async job with the customer polled/pushed to once resolved. Given these are rare (a few/day) and the actual bug is customers seeing a wrong status, I'd go async — it fixes the false "failed" directly and stops flaky requests from making the checkout endpoint itself slower.

For a few-word query matching name/description, the fork is scale: under ~100k products, Postgres full-text search (`tsvector` column with a GIN index, weighted so name ranks above description) is enough and avoids a new service. Past that, or once you want typo tolerance and fast ranked relevance, move to a dedicated search index like Typesense or Elasticsearch, fed by a change-stream or nightly sync from the product table.

Either way: debounce the input, hit an API endpoint that does prefix + trigram matching (`pg_trgm` if staying on Postgres), and return top-N ranked by relevance with name matches weighted over description matches. Indexing strategy and how fresh results need to be after a product edit are the details below that.

Approach: client resizes/compresses the photo before upload (phone shots run 3-12MB at 4000×3000+; downscale to something like 2048px long edge, JPEG ~80%, and convert HEIC to JPEG since Android/browsers can't render it), then the client uploads directly to object storage (S3/GCS/R2) via a presigned URL your server issues rather than proxying the bytes through your app server. On completion the client calls your API to attach the resulting object key to the listing; a background job then generates thumbnail/display variants (grid, detail, full) rather than doing that inline on upload.

Two decisions that actually fork this:
- **Presigned direct upload vs. proxy through your server** — direct is far cheaper/faster and avoids tying up app-server workers on large uploads, but you lose the chance to validate/moderate content before it lands in storage (do that check async after upload, before the photo goes live on the listing).
- **Mobile network reliability** — cellular uploads drop mid-transfer; you want per-file retry with backoff and (for larger galleries) resumable/chunked upload rather than restarting a failed multi-MB upload from zero.

Left out: multi-photo ordering/reordering UI, EXIF orientation/GPS stripping, and the moderation/abuse pipeline — all real but secondary to the upload path itself.

Extend the same pattern already used for `quota_exceeded`: alerts are data that `govern()` emits, and the supervisor (the only I/O-capable layer) just dispatches whatever comes back. Two decisions actually fork the design:

- **Guardrail vs. alert are different shapes.** Guardrails are single-winner (first match in priority order), but several alert conditions — cap pinned two cycles, pace error above 15% two cycles — can be true regardless of which guardrail "won" that cycle. So `govern()` needs to return an `alerts: []` list separate from `result.guardrail`, and the "N consecutive cycles" counters (stale, pinned, pace-error) belong in the persisted state so they replay correctly through the simulation harness, same as everything else in `state`.
- **Heartbeat-missed can't come from `govern()` at all.** If the loop doesn't run, nothing calls it — there's no result to inspect. That one needs an external watchdog: something outside the per-tenant control loop that checks "did tenant X get a cycle recorded in the last 5 minutes," using the cycle-record from step 4. It's a different component with a different failure mode (absence, not a bad value).

Left out: actual alert transport (paging/Slack/dedup/throttling) — that's a level down and doesn't affect the core design.

Every write in this service already funnels through one function — `db.write()` in `db.js`, which wraps each call in its own transaction. That chokepoint is where I'd hook the audit trail, rather than instrumenting each route.

**The one fork that matters: trigger-based vs. application-level capture.**

- App-level (insert an audit row from inside `write()`) is easy to make rich — you can log the route/endpoint, the intent, whatever — but it only fires for writes that go through this code path. Anyone doing a manual `UPDATE` in a psql session or a future migration script leaves no trail.
- DB-level (Postgres triggers) capture every row change no matter who or what makes it, including out-of-band admin fixes. That's stronger for a compliance guarantee, but a trigger doesn't know "who" — the pool connects as one shared DB role, so `current_user` is useless for attribution.

I'd combine them: a generic `AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE` trigger on each audited table that writes `(table, row_id, action, old_row, new_row, at)` as jsonb into an append-only `audit_log`, plus a one-line addition at the top of `db.write()`'s transaction — `SET LOCAL app.actor_id = $1` — so the trigger can read `current_setting('app.actor_id')` and attach the actor. That gets you "what and when" guaranteed at the DB level, and "who" threaded from the single place all app writes already pass through.

Two gaps this surfaces in the current code, worth knowing about even though I haven't touched anything:
- `req.user` (set by `auth.js` on every request) never reaches `db.write()` today — nothing currently identifies the actor for a write. You'd need to pass it in (explicit param, or `AsyncLocalStorage` keyed per-request so call sites don't all need updating).
- `audit_log` needs to actually be append-only — revoke `UPDATE`/`DELETE` grants on it from the app's DB role, otherwise "audit trail" is just another mutable table.

Depth I'd leave for a follow-up: retention/rotation policy, and whether compliance wants row-level diffs or just before/after full snapshots.

Cache-aside in Redis, keyed by product ID, is the right shape here: on a page request, check Redis first, fall back to the DB on miss, write the result back with a TTL. Product pages are read-heavy and change infrequently (price, stock, description), so this alone should collapse most of that 900ms to a few ms on hits.

Two decisions actually fork the design:

1. **Invalidation: TTL-only vs event-driven.** A short TTL (30-60s) is simplest and tolerates stale stock/price briefly. If that staleness is unacceptable (e.g., price changes must be immediate), invalidate the key on write instead — whatever updates the product row also deletes/refreshes its cache entry. Pick TTL unless you have a concrete case where stale data causes a real problem.
2. **What layer to cache at.** Caching the assembled page (or its DB query results) in Redis is the first move; if the page is largely the same for all visitors (no per-user pricing/cart state), fronting it with a CDN/edge cache is a bigger win since it skips your app server entirely, not just the DB.

What's the stack (any cache already in place, e.g. Redis/Memcached available), and is any part of the page personalized per user?

Key by `client_id`, not IP — `routes/api.js` already resolves `req.client.client_id` and `plan` in the auth middleware, and the comment above it says clients can share a NAT or call from many addresses, so IP-based limiting would both punish innocent neighbors and let the offender dodge it by rotating source IPs.

State has to live in Redis, not process memory: `app.js` clusters 4 workers per box with nothing shared in module scope, and `redis.js` is already the one store every worker and every box has in common (it's doing this job for sessions today). Add a small middleware in `routes/api.js`, right after the auth middleware sets `req.client` and before the route handlers hit Postgres — that's what's actually getting hammered, so the limiter needs to sit in front of it, not after. On an over-limit request, short-circuit with `429` and a `Retry-After` header rather than letting it reach `db.query`.

For the counter itself, use a Lua script (`EVAL`) that does the increment-and-check atomically in Redis — plain `INCR` then `EXPIRE` as two round trips races under concurrent requests from multiple workers and lets a burst slip through right at the window boundary. Two ways to shape it, and this is the one real fork: a fixed-window counter (`INCR` a `ratelimit:{client_id}:{windowBucket}` key, cap it, TTL the key) is a few lines and cheap, but allows up to 2x the limit across a window edge; a token-bucket/GCRA script is a bit more code but rejects sustained hammering smoothly without that edge case. Given the complaint is sustained abuse degrading everyone else, not an occasional burst, token bucket is the better fit here. Limits should read from `req.client.plan`, which is already fetched, so tiers fall out for free.

Left out, worth deciding before building: what the middleware does if Redis itself is unreachable (fail-open avoids an outage taking down `/v1`, fail-closed avoids the exact hammering scenario during a Redis blip), and the actual per-plan numbers.

The platform doc rules out the obvious answers: no WebSockets (connection upgrades 501 at the edge), no SSE either (a function is frozen/killed within 10s, so it can't hold a stream open), and no shared memory between instances to coordinate a push. Polling is the only option this platform supports.

Since `rollup` only changes once a minute via the scheduled job, poll `/api/metrics` on a timer in `public/dashboard.js` instead of only on click/load — e.g. every 60s, ideally with a small random offset so all open tabs don't hit the ingest job's write window at the same instant. Compare the returned `computed_at` to the last-seen value and skip `render()` when it hasn't changed, so a poll that lands between rewrites doesn't cause a flicker. Keep the "Refresh" button calling the same `load()` for a manual override, and gate the interval with the Page Visibility API so backgrounded tabs stop polling.

That's it — no infrastructure change, just replacing the click-only handler with `setInterval(load, 60000)` plus the `computed_at` guard.

The trap here is in `PROVIDER.md`: a timeout is explicitly "unknown," never "failed" — the request may have already authorised. Retrying blindly (as `checkout.js` would need to, since `payments.js` has no idempotency key today) risks charging the customer twice. So retrying isn't just "call charge() again" — it has to be idempotency-key-first:

1. **Persist an idempotency key on the order before the first attempt.** Derive it from the order id (one order, one intended charge) and write it to the `orders` row in the same statement that moves status to something like `pending_payment`, before calling `payments.charge`. That makes the key stable across retries and survivable across a process crash, not just a local retry loop.
2. **Send `Idempotency-Key` on every attempt for that order, including retries.** A retry with the same key either returns the original charge (if it went through) or authorises exactly once (if it didn't) — never both.
3. **Retry only on timeout/`req.on('error')`, not on a 4xx from the provider.** A decline is a real, final answer; retrying it is pointless and could confuse dispute handling. Bound it (e.g. 2–3 attempts, short backoff) — rate limit is a non-issue at 600/min.
4. **Stop saying "payment failed" for this path.** `checkout.js`'s catch-all `502 payment failed` is wrong for a timeout: it invites the customer to retry with a new card while an authorisation may be sitting live against their old one. Exhausting retries should land the order in a distinct state (`payment_pending`/unknown), not `failed`.
5. **Something has to resolve state 4 eventually**, since synchronous retries can time out too — a background job that keeps replaying the same idempotency-keyed request (or checks status, if the vendor exposes that) until it gets a definitive charge id or a genuine decline.

The fork I can't resolve for you: whether the bounded retries (point 3) happen synchronously inside the `/pay` request (simple, but ties up the request for up to ~30s at 3×10s) or the handler returns "processing" immediately and a worker does all the retrying async. I'd lean synchronous-first-then-async-fallback, but that's a latency/UX call, not a technical one. Backoff timing and the reconciliation worker's own schedule are the next level down.

**Recommended flow:** presigned direct-to-storage upload, not a proxy through your app server. Backend issues a short-lived presigned URL (S3/GCS/Azure Blob) for the client to PUT to directly — phone camera photos run 3-12MB each, and routing that through your API server just to relay bytes doesn't scale and adds latency.

**Two decisions that shape it:**

1. **Client-side resize before upload.** Have the client downscale/compress via canvas (e.g. cap at ~2000px longest edge, JPEG ~85%) before the PUT. This cuts upload time on cellular and avoids storing bloated originals. Skipping this and uploading raw phone photos works but costs you bandwidth and storage for no real benefit — sellers don't need 12MP originals served back.
2. **Async variant generation.** After upload, don't block the UI on processing — create the photo row in a `pending` state, fire a job (queue + worker, or storage-trigger like S3 event → Lambda) that generates thumbnail/display/full sizes, strips EXIF (especially GPS), and flips the row to `ready`. The listing UI shows a placeholder/spinner per photo until ready.

Depth I'm leaving out: content moderation/malware scanning on upload, resumable/retry logic for flaky mobile connections, and photo ordering/reordering UX — worth designing once the core flow is picked, but they don't fork the architecture above.

Alerting should live entirely in the supervisor, as a step after `govern()` returns — not inside `govern()` itself. That's the one fork this spec really turns on: core purity (SPEC.md:35-42) is what makes the simulation harness replay thousands of cycles/sec, so alert dispatch (network I/O) can't leak into the pure core. The cycle pseudocode at SPEC.md:31-32 already shows the pattern (`if result.guardrail == "quota_exceeded": alert(...)`) — generalize that into a small guardrail→alert map for `quota_exceeded`, `floor_at_risk`, `floor_unreachable`, and `config_invalid`, fired straight off `result.guardrail` each cycle.

Two of the eight conditions (SPEC.md:64-73) don't reduce to "guardrail fired this cycle" and need their own handling:

- **Consecutive-cycle conditions** — `feed_stale` past three cycles, cap pinned at a band edge for two cycles, pace error >15% for two cycles. These need small counters in the persisted controller state, incremented/reset by the supervisor from `result.guardrail`/`result.cap`/computed pace error, alerting only when a counter crosses its threshold. (The feed_stale counter can likely reuse whatever state `govern()` already tracks for its own three-cycle fallback, per SPEC.md:50-52.)
- **Heartbeat missed** — the loop that would raise this alert is the thing that isn't running, so it can't self-report. This needs an external watchdog: something outside the supervisor (a dead-man's-switch check, or metrics-based alerting on "no cycle recorded for tenant X in >5 min") that pages when an expected heartbeat doesn't arrive.

Left out at this depth: alert delivery/dedup mechanics (paging system, rate-limiting repeated fires) and exact threshold wiring for the two counters — those are implementation details, not forks.

This service has one real chokepoint already: every write goes through `db.write()` in db.js:13-26, which is also the only place a transaction begins, and every request already has `req.user` resolved by `sessionUser` in auth.js:5-13. That's where I'd anchor the audit trail rather than adding logging calls to each route.

**Recommend: Postgres triggers, not application-level logging calls.** A generic `AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE` trigger function (using `TG_TABLE_NAME`, `TG_OP`, `row_to_json(OLD)`/`row_to_json(NEW)`) attached to each audited table writes to an `audit_log` table automatically. The reason to prefer this over logging inside route handlers: it can't be forgotten. Route handlers here build raw SQL and call `db.write()` directly (routes/accounts.js:7, routes/orders.js:7,15) — any new route added later that skips a deliberate "log this" call silently produces a gap, and a trigger doesn't have that failure mode.

**The one thing triggers can't see is "who."** Postgres session variables solve it: have `db.write()` run `SET LOCAL app.user_id = $1` (and `app.user_email`) as the first statement inside its existing `BEGIN`/`COMMIT` (db.js:16-18), sourced from `req.user`. The trigger reads it back with `current_setting('app.user_id', true)`. Since `write()` is the single chokepoint, this is a one-line addition there instead of touching accounts.js/orders.js. Threading `req.user` into `write()` without editing every call site is the other real decision — either add it as a parameter now, or use `AsyncLocalStorage` set once in `sessionUser` so `write()` can read it implicitly.

**Schema:** `audit_log(id, table_name, row_pk, action, actor_id, actor_email, before jsonb, after jsonb, changed_at timestamptz default now())`. Denormalize `actor_email` at write time since users can be deleted later and the trail must still read.

**Immutability matters for compliance, not just capture.** Revoke `UPDATE`/`DELETE` on `audit_log` from the app's DB role so it's insert-only even if app credentials are compromised — otherwise the trail itself isn't trustworthy as evidence.

Left out: retention/export policy, and there's currently no request id/IP captured anywhere in this app for forensic correlation — that'd need to go in the session variable alongside actor id if you want it.

Two decisions actually fork this:

**Is the page the same for every visitor, or personalized (logged-in pricing, inventory per account, etc.)?** If it's the same for everyone, cache the whole rendered page at the CDN/edge (Cloudflare, Fastly, or a reverse proxy like Varnish) keyed by product ID — that's the biggest win since it skips your app entirely. If it's personalized, you can't cache the page, so cache the expensive DB reads themselves (product row, price, inventory, reviews) in Redis/Memcached keyed by product ID, and still render per-request.

**Invalidation: TTL or write-triggered?** A short TTL (30–120s) is simplest and tolerates a bit of staleness — fine for things like "related products" or descriptions. For price/inventory, invalidate explicitly on write (delete the cache key when the product is updated) rather than waiting out a TTL, since stale prices are the kind of bug that gets noticed.

Given it's "nearly all the database," the fastest fix regardless of the above is a data-layer cache in front of the specific slow queries (Redis, keyed by product ID, TTL + write-invalidation) — that alone should collapse most of the 900ms without touching rendering. Full-page/edge caching is the next tier if the page turns out to be non-personalized.

Token bucket keyed by API key (not IP — shared IPs and NAT would punish innocent clients sharing one), enforced as close to the edge as possible so the offending client's requests get shot down before they burn shared capacity. Add a global concurrency cap as backstop so even a client under its own quota can't starve others during a burst. On limit hit: 429 with a `Retry-After` header.

The fork that actually matters: is this one process or several? Single instance, an in-memory bucket per key is enough. Multiple instances/load-balanced, the counters need to live somewhere shared (Redis is the standard choice, atomic via a Lua script or `INCR`+`EXPIRE`) or each client can burst past the limit by hitting a different instance each time.

What's the stack here — gateway/proxy in front of /v1 (nginx, Envoy, Kong), or is this enforced in application middleware? That decides whether this is a config change or a code change.

Given the constraints in `PLATFORM.md`, this rules out the usual answer:

- No WebSockets — connection upgrades 501 at the edge.
- No SSE either — functions are frozen/killed at 10s and there's no sticky routing, so a held-open response can't outlive one instance anyway.
- Data only changes once a minute (`jobs/rollup.md`), and `api/metrics.js` already tells you exactly when, via `computed_at`.

So this is just polling, done right: replace the click handler in `public/dashboard.js` with `setInterval(load, 15000)` or so — anything sub-minute is fine since `Cache-Control: no-store` means every call hits the real rollup. The one decision that actually forks the design: whether to poll blindly or poll-and-compare using `computed_at`. Blind polling re-renders every tick even when nothing changed; comparing the new `computed_at` against the last-seen value before calling `render()` avoids that and also lets you show "last updated" accurately instead of just "last fetched." Given the 1/minute cadence, I'd do the latter — it's a few extra lines in `load()`, not a new endpoint.

Depth left out: backoff/retry behavior if a poll fails, and whether to pause polling on a hidden tab (`document.visibilityState`) to cut idle requests.
